items.descriptionOriginal: Τι μπορεί να ενώσει εκατοντάδες χιλιόμετρα δύσβατων διαδρομών στα βουνά της Βόρειας Ελλάδας, από τη Νυμφαία Ροδόπης μέχρι τα Άνω Πορόια Σερρών, με ενδιάμεσους σταθμούς σε περιοχές των νομών Ξάνθης και Δράμας; Στη διαδρομή των 517 χιλιομέτρων που σχεδίασε και διέτρεξε σε διάστημα 15 ημερών ένας γενικός χειρουργός από τη Θεσσαλονίκη, δίνεται η απάντηση. Πρόκειται για ένα δρομικό εγχείρημα που έκανε στα ίχνη της Γραμμής Μεταξά , θέλοντας να θυμίσει τους ανθρώπους που την υπερασπίστηκαν τον Απρίλιο του 1941. Πρόκειται για τον Στέργιο Αράπογλου, ο οποίος ξεκίνησε στις 3 Οκτωβρίου, στις 7 το πρωί, από το οχυρό Νυμφαία, το ανατολικότερο οχυρό της Γραμμής Μεταξά, και ολοκλήρωσε το εγχείρημά του στις 18 Οκτωβρίου, φτάνοντας στο Πολυβολείο 9, πάνω από τα Άνω Πορόια του νομού Σερρών. Στη διαδρομή του πέρασε από συνολικά 21 οχυρά και πολυβολεία στους νομούς Ροδόπης, Ξάνθης, Δράμας και Σερρών. Παρότι έχει πραγματοποιήσει στο παρελθόν εγχειρήματα πολύ μεγαλύτερων αποστάσεων, ο ίδιος χαρακτηρίζει αυτήν τη διαδρομή ως τη δυσκολότερη που έχει επιχειρήσει. « Έπρεπε να ανέβω και να κατέβω στα βουνά πολλές φορές, σε σημεία δυσπρόσιτα, υπό ακραίες συνθήκες πολλές φορές. Ήταν μέρη εγκαταλειμμένα, επικίνδυνα, με πολλή μοναξιά και άγρια ζώα, όπως αγριογούρουνα, λύκους και αρκούδες », λέει στο Αθηναϊκό-Μακεδονικό Πρακτορείο Ειδήσεων. Ο κ. Αράπογλου έτρεχε μόνος του, όπως και στα προηγούμενα μεγάλα εγχειρήματά του. Ένας φίλος τον υποστήριζε με αυτοκίνητο στα σημεία όπου υπήρχε οδικό δίκτυο, ενώ όταν η διαδρομή ανέβαινε στο βουνό, οι δύο άνδρες έδιναν ραντεβού στο σημείο όπου εκείνος θα κατέβαινε ξανά. Τα βράδια, έχοντας ήδη ολοκληρώσει τον ημερήσιο στόχο του, διανυκτέρευε σε μικρά ξενοδοχεία της επαρχίας, τα οποία είχαν κλειστεί εκ των προτέρων, και το επόμενο πρωί ξεκινούσε και πάλι. Η διαδρομή, ωστόσο, δεν σχεδιάστηκε απλώς πάνω σε έναν χάρτη . Ο ίδιος την είχε μελετήσει πολλές φορές πριν από την εκκίνηση. « Κάθε φορά κάνω λεπτομερή κατόπτευση της διαδρομής, πηγαίνω τη βλέπω από κοντά και την υλοποιώ στη συνέχεια. Είχα έτοιμα σενάρια για το πώς θα αντιμετωπίσω οτιδήποτε μπορεί να μου βγάλει το σώμα μου ή κάποια αναποδιά με τον καιρό. Ήμουν προετοιμασμένος για τα πάντα» , εξηγεί. Η ιδέα που γεννήθηκε στο Ρούπελ Η ιδέα για τη συγκεκριμένη διαδρομή γεννήθηκε το 2022, όταν ο γενικός χειρουργός σχεδίαζε το προηγούμενο μεγάλο εγχείρημά του και πέρασε από το οχυρό Ρούπελ. Εκεί συναντήθηκε με τον υπεύθυνο του οχυρού, αντισυνταγματάρχη Νικόλαο Γκιρμπάτση, και η συζήτησή τους έμελλε να αποτελέσει την αφετηρία για το εγχείρημα που ολοκλήρωσε πριν λίγες μέρες. « Μου είπε ότι κάνει τη διδακτορική του διατριβή με θέμα τα οχυρά της Γραμμής Μεταξά, όπου ψάχνει και ξαναβρίσκει όλα τα πολυβολεία, τα καταγράφει και πρακτικά ξανακάνει τα σχέδια των οχυρών της Γραμμής Μεταξά, τα οποία είχαν χαθεί », αναφέρε Ο Στέργιος Αράπογλου σκέφτηκε ότι αυτή η έρευνα θα μπορούσε να αξιοποιηθεί με τον δικό του τρόπο: να σχεδιάσει μια διαδρομή που θα ένωνε σε μια νοητή γραμμή τα οχυρά και τα πολυβολεία και να τη διατρέξει με τα πόδια. Δεν ήταν η πρώτη φορά που μετέτρεπε μια μεγάλη αθλητική διαδρομή σε όχημα για ένα κοινωνικό και ιστορικό μήνυμα. Το 2023 είχε διανύσει 3.064 χιλιόμετρα, από τον Έβρο έως την Κρήτη, περνώντας από 65 μνημεία ολοκαυτωμάτων, με στόχο να αναδείξει τη μνήμη των θυμάτων των ναζιστικών θηριωδιών και το ζήτημα των γερμανικών οφειλών. Όπως εξηγεί, από το 2012, οπότε και σταμάτησε να συμμετέχει σε αγώνες υπεραποστάσεων, σχεδιάζει ο ίδιος διαδρομές εκατοντάδων ή και χιλιάδων χιλιομέτρων, στις οποίες το τρέξιμο αποτελεί το μέσο για να αναδείξει κάθε φορά μια διαφορετική ιστορία. Στα οχυρά ακούστηκαν τα ονόματα των νεκρών Για τη Γραμμή Μεταξά, ο κ. Αράπογλου μιλά με ιδιαίτερη φόρτιση. Θεωρεί ότι πρόκειται για το μεγαλύτερο τεχνικό οχυρωματικό κατασκευαστικό έργο του 20ού αιώνα στην Ελλάδα, το οποίο, όπως υπογραμμίζει, « έγινε αμιγώς με ελληνικά σχέδια και ελληνικά χέρια… ». Πάνω απ’ όλα όμως, τον ενδιαφέρουν οι άνθρωποι που κλήθηκαν να το υπερασπιστούν. Ήταν, όπως λέει, στρατιώτες από κάθε γωνιά της Ελλάδας, πολλοί από τους οποίους δεν γνώριζαν καν πού ακριβώς βρίσκονταν κοντά στα ελληνοβουλγαρικά σύνορα. Εκεί, τον Απρίλιο του 1941, βρέθηκαν απέναντι στη γερμανική πολεμική μηχανή, με την αεροπορία, το πυροβολικό και τις μεραρχίες της να επιχειρούν να διασπάσουν τη Γραμμή Μεταξά. « Αυτοί λοιπόν δεν δίστασαν να σταθούν απέναντι στη μεγαλύτερη πολεμική μηχανή εκείνης της εποχής », λέει χαρακτηριστικά. Για τον λόγο αυτό, στο συγκεκριμένο εγχείρημα ο κ. Αράπογλου αποφάσισε να δώσει πρωταγωνιστικό ρόλο στους ανθρώπους αυτούς . Αναζήτησε στα αρχεία της Διεύθυνσης Ιστορίας Στρατού τα ονόματα των φονευθέντων και των εξαφανισθέντων και τα οργάνωσε ανά οχυρό, ώστε κάθε φορά που έφτανε σε ένα από αυτά να μπορεί να αναφερθεί όχι μόνο στην ιστορία του, αλλά και στους ανθρώπους που χάθηκαν εκεί. Έτσι, στα βουνά της Ροδόπης, της Ξάνθης, της Δράμας και των Σερρών, η διαδρομή μετατράπηκε σε ένα διαδοχικό προσκλητήριο. « Περνώντας από κάθε οχυρό, καθώς έτρεχα, έκανα ένα μικρό βίντεο όπου έλεγα συνοπτικά την ιστορία του, πότε κατασκευάστηκε, ποια ήταν η αποστολή του, πόσα άτομα το επάνδρωναν και τι ακριβώς συνέβη εκεί. Στη συνέχεια έκανα το προσκλητήριο των φονευθέντων και των εξαφανισθέντων », σημειώνει. Τα βίντεο δημοσιεύονταν σχεδόν σε πραγματικό χρόνο στα κοινωνικά του δίκτυα , ενώ η διαδρομή του καταγραφόταν συνεχώς από δύο συσκευές GPS και μπορούσε να παρακολουθείται ζωντανά μέσω διαδικτύου. Η δημοσιοποίηση της πορείας του είχε ως αποτέλεσμα άνθρωποι από τις περιοχές από τις οποίες περνούσε να αναζητούν τον δρομέα και να σπεύδουν να τον συναντήσουν. « Κάνοντας αυτήν τη διαδρομή με αυτόν τον τρόπο, πρακτικά έγινε ένα ταξίδι μνήμης . Πολλά από τα προσκλητήρια έγιναν σε κορυφές, σε κορυφογραμμές, και ήταν ένα μνημόσυνο. Επειδή ακούστηκαν όλα τα ονόματα, ήταν σαν να ξαναζωντάνευε η διμοιρία αυτών των ανθρώπων, τους οποίους εν πολλοίς, ακόμα κι εμείς οι μεγαλύτεροι, τους έχουμε ξεχάσει », επισημαίνει. Συγκινεί η ιστορία των εξαφανισθέντων Ανάμεσα σε όλους εκείνους που αναζήτησε στα αρχεία, ιδιαίτερη συγκίνηση του προκαλούν οι εξαφανισθέντες . Πρόκειται, όπως λέει, σε πολλές περιπτώσεις, για στρατιώτες που επάνδρωναν τα προκεχωρημένα φυλάκια και τις θέσεις προκαλύψεως, βρίσκονταν δηλαδή στην πρώτη γραμμή όταν ξεκίνησε η γερμανική επίθεση στις 6 Απριλίου 1941. « Όταν στις 5:15 το πρωί της 6ης Απριλίου άρχισαν οι Γερμανοί να βάλλουν με το πυροβολικό, με τις πρώτες οβίδες, αυτοί κυριολεκτικά εξαϋλώθηκαν. Όταν είσαι σε ένα όρυγμα και σου έρχεται μία οβίδα 88 χιλιοστών ευθυτενούς τροχιάς, πώς να γλιτώσεις; » αναρωτιέται. Οι άνθρωποι αυτοί δεν άφησαν πίσω τους έναν τάφο, ένα σημείο στο οποίο θα μπορούσαν να σταθούν οι συγγενείς τους για να τους θυμηθούν. Για δεκαετίες, σε πολλές περιπτώσεις, παρέμειναν απλώς ως ονόματα στα αρχεία. « Ποτέ, μέχρι και σήμερα, 85 χρόνια μετά, δεν μπορεί κανείς να ξέρει πού είναι, πού βρίσκονται », τονίζει. Αυτή ακριβώς η απουσία, όπως την αντιλαμβάνεται ο ίδιος, ήταν που έδωσε ιδιαίτερο βάρος στο προσκλητήριο που έκανε στα οχυρά. Παρά το γεγονός ότι ο ίδιος ασχολείται εδώ και χρόνια με την ελληνική ιστορία και έχει μελετήσει εκτενώς τα γεγονότα της περιόδου, υποστηρίζει ότι ακόμη και σήμερα υπάρχουν σημαντικά κενά στον τρόπο με τον οποίο παρουσιάζεται η μάχη των οχυρών. « Η μάχη των οχυρών της Γραμμής Μεταξά δεν βρίσκεται ακόμα και σήμερα που μιλάμε σε κανένα επίσημο επιστημονικό σύγγραμμα της Ελλάδας. Έχει μόνο καταγραφεί από μεμονωμένους συγγραφείς που ασχολήθηκαν με το θέμα », υποστηρίζει. Για τον ίδιο, η ιστορική μνήμη, εκτός από την αναφορά στα γεγονότα, αφορά και στην ανάδειξη των προσώπων που τα έζησαν. Σε αυτό το πλαίσιο εντάσσει και ορισμένες από τις μεμονωμένες ιστορίες στρατιωτών που συνάντησε κατά την έρευνά του και οι οποίες, όπως λέει, τον συγκίνησαν ιδιαίτερα. Πρόκειται για ανθρώπους τους οποίους θεωρεί πρότυπα ζωής και οι οποίοι, κατά την άποψή του, έδειξαν σε ακραίες συνθήκες τι μπορεί να σημαίνει η προσήλωση σε μια αξία. « Κανένας και τίποτα δεν μπορεί να είναι πάνω από τη σημαία μας. Και όταν βάζουμε σωστά πρότυπα και τα ακολουθούμε, η σημαία μας δεν υποστέλλεται ποτέ», δηλώνει. «Δεν είμαι εγώ ο πρωταγωνιστής» Ο Στέργιος Αράπογλου είναι μάχιμος γενικός χειρουργός στο Ιπποκράτειο Νοσοκομείο Θεσσαλονίκης εδώ και 25 χρόνια. Το τρέξιμο μεγάλων αποστάσεων αποτελεί ένα σημαντικό κομμάτι της ζωής του, με δεκάδες μαραθωνίους και υπερμαραθωνίους, αλλά και εγχειρήματα που ξεπερνούν κατά πολύ τις συνηθισμένες αθλητικές προκλήσεις. Το 2018 διέσχισε ολόκληρη την ηπειρωτική Ελλάδα, από το Ορμένιο Έβρου έως το Ακρωτήριο Ταίναρον, διανύοντας 1.519 χιλιόμετρα σε 23 ημέρες. Το 2023 έφτασε τα 3.064 χιλιόμετρα. Η φετινή διαδρομή ήταν μικρότερη αριθμητικά, αλλά, όπως ο ίδιος υποστηρίζει, περισσότερο απαιτητική από πολλές προηγούμενες. Την ολοκλήρωσε χωρίς χορηγούς, όπως έχει κάνει και στα προηγούμενα εγχειρήματά του, καλύπτοντας ο ίδιος τα έξοδα και επιμένοντας ότι η προσωπική του προσπάθεια δεν πρέπει να επισκιάζει τον λόγο για τον οποίο πραγματοποιείται. « Δεν είμαι εγώ ο πρωταγωνιστής. Πρωταγωνιστές είναι οι αγνοούμενοι, οι φονευθέντες και οι οικογένειές τους », σημειώνει. Για τον ίδιο, ένα τέτοιο εγχείρημα απαιτεί πέντε πράγματα: «μέταλλο», πίστη στο όραμα, ψυχή, καρδιά και βαθιά γνώση. Το πρώτο αφορά τον χαρακτήρα και την ικανότητα να παραμένει κανείς σταθερός όταν έρχονται οι δυσκολίες. Η πίστη αφορά το ίδιο το όραμα που έχει δημιουργήσει. Η ψυχή είναι το θάρρος απέναντι στον φόβο και στις αναποδιές, η καρδιά η σωματική αντοχή και η γνώση η λεπτομερής προετοιμασία για κάθε πτυχή της διαδρομής. Όλα αυτά, όμως, έχουν για τον ίδιο αξία μόνο εφόσον μπορούν να μεταφερθούν και στους άλλους, με τρόπο απλό και κατανοητό. Ειδήσεις σήμερα Μεγάλη κινητοποίηση των εργαζομένων στα δημόσια νοσοκομεία – Τι ζητούν Ο άγνωστος διαβήτης που «χτυπά» εκατομμύρια νέους και αδύνατους – Γιατί διχάζει τους επιστήμονες Ιός Έμπολα: Το ECDC στέλνει ειδικούς στη Νιγηρία – Πολύ χαμηλός ο κίνδυνος για την Ευρώπη

items.descriptionOriginal: Cars are a big reason city air is so grimy, and not just because of what comes out of the tailpipe. Researchers in South Korea now want to turn them into massive Roombas for city air, with a grille that scrubs roadside air as the car drives and a catcher that grabs brake dust where it's made. items.descriptionOriginal: Κάποιοι οργανώνουν κάθε λεπτομέρεια πριν κάνουν το επόμενο βήμα. Άλλοι αναζητούν διαρκώς καινούργιες εμπειρίες. Μερικοί εμπιστεύονται εύκολα τους ανθρώπους, ενώ άλλοι ανησυχούν ακόμη και όταν όλα μοιάζουν να πηγαίνουν καλά. Πίσω από αυτές τις διαφορές στους χαρακτήρες κρύβεται ένα ερώτημα που μας αφορά όλους: Πόσο από αυτό που είμαστε το έχουμε κληρονομήσει και πόσο το έχουμε διαμορφώσει στην πορεία της ζωής μας; Μελέτη που δημοσιεύθηκε στο επιστημονικό περιοδικό Nature, αξιοποιώντας δεδομένα από περισσότερους από ένα εκατομμύριο ανθρώπους, προσφέρει μια λεπτομερή εικόνα της γενετικής βάσης της προσωπικότητας. Οι επιστήμονες εντόπισαν εκατοντάδες γενετικές παραλλαγές που συνδέονται με τον χαρακτήρα μας. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age Reading Time: 3 minutes From picture books for toddlers to a 400-page field guide, new bat conservation books invite readers of every age into the surprisingly wondrous world of the only flying mammal. Bat conservation books rarely dominate bestseller lists, but a fresh crop of titles released this year proves the subject deserves far more shelf space than it typically gets. Bat Conservation International recently rounded up a dozen standout titles spanning children’s picture books to dense scientific references, each aiming to replace fear of bats with fascination. For younger readers, several bat conservation books lean into storytelling and gentle life lessons. Stellaluna, considered among the first children’s books centered on bats, follows a baby fruit bat raised temporarily among birds after falling from her mother’s roost, ultimately learning that differences need not prevent friendship. I’m Not Scary follows a lonely bat who simply wants companionship despite living somewhere admittedly spooky, offering warm illustrations built around a familiar theme: kindness overcoming fear. Other bat conservation books for children tackle real conservation challenges directly. Bat Count: A Citizen Science Story introduces young readers to white-nose syndrome, the disease that has devastated North American bat populations, following a girl preparing for a community bat count who learns both the crisis facing bats and how ordinary people can help through citizen science. Amara and the Bats follows a similar arc, as a young bat enthusiast discovers her new neighborhood’s bat roosts have vanished due to tree removal, then finds inspiration in other young people already working to protect local bat populations. Additional titles for younger audiences round out the reading list. Little Red Bat explores the dilemma facing bat species that must choose between migration and hibernation as autumn arrives, weaving in facts about tree-roosting habits and camouflage along the way. The Bat Book, narrated from the perspective of a juvenile bat living under a bridge in Austin, Texas, directly addresses common misconceptions children repeat about bats being weird or scary. For adult readers and dedicated naturalists, bat conservation books shift toward deeper scientific territory. The Secret Lives of Bats follows renowned bat photographer and biologist Merlin Tuttle’s decades-long career, beginning with a teenage cave discovery outside Knoxville, Tennessee, that launched a lifetime devoted to bat ecology and conservation across encounters ranging from Kentucky moonshiners to charging elephants. The Weird and Wonderful World of Bats takes a curiosity-driven approach, devoting individual chapters to each bat sense, including echolocation, alongside candid explorations of bat mating behavior and social communication. For naturalists and dedicated readers, recent bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family and Bat Island document the diversity of nearly 1,500 known bat species through detailed photography, distribution maps, and firsthand field research. Photo courtesy of Bat Conservation International . The Genius Bat follows an ecologist’s research travels from Israeli deserts to tropical rainforests, examining how scientists design experiments to study bats’ extraordinary sensory and behavioral adaptations. For readers wanting comprehensive identification resources, bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family organize the roughly 1,500 known bat species by suborder, pairing close-up photography with distribution maps and details on diet, anatomy, and physiology. Bat Island narrows its focus dramatically, documenting the 76 bat species found on a single small island in Panama’s Lake Gatun through cinematic photography and firsthand research from Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute scientists. Rounding out the collection, Bats: An Illustrated Guide to All Species offers a 400-page reference dividing global bat diversity along modern phylogenetic lines, paired with extensive photography documenting species across every studied region. Together, these bat conservation books reflect a broader shift in how bats are represented in popular literature, moving decisively away from Halloween-season stereotypes toward genuine appreciation for animals that pollinate plants, disperse seeds, and consume enormous quantities of agricultural pests nightly. Whether introducing a child to their first bat-loving picture book character or offering seasoned naturalists a comprehensive species reference, this year’s releases make clear that meaningful conservation storytelling can also be genuinely engaging reading, proving that getting curious about bats might be the easiest first step toward protecting them. The post Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Το πείραμα του Business School χωρίς τιμές
items.titleOriginal: The Business School Experiment with No Prices
items.description: Νωρίς στο σχολείο, ο Gaurav Marathe αγκάλιασε ένα μάντρα Viraja που μεταφράστηκε από έναν δάσκαλο: "Οι άνθρωποι είναι σαν ένα κερί. Αφού καεί το κερί, ο άνθρακας μένει πάνω του, και πρέπει να αφαιρέσετε αυτόν τον μαύρο άνθρακα από το φως, ώστε το φως να ανάψει ξανά." Το μάντρα του έμαθε να πειραματίζεται τόσο με την αφαίρεση του άνθρακα όσο και με το φωτισμό του jyoti -- το φως…
items.descriptionOriginal: Early on in school, Gaurav Marathe embraced a Viraja mantra translated by a teacher: "Humans are like a candle. After the candle burns, carbon stays on it, and you have to remove that black carbon from the light so the light again illuminates." The mantra taught him to experiment with both removing the carbon and illuminating the jyoti -- the light that exists within. In one of many experiments, he challenged students to remove the carbon of a task-driven, rule-driven festival on a campus where he taught. "Let's do that experiment. Let it be the kind of carnival where nobody is charging anything. No cost price, nothing. If anybody wants to pay, they pay. If they don't, they don't. Let's believe in that spirit." It was successful beyond anyone's imagination, and became a "Soul Carnival" where the focus is on giving over profiting. "Perhaps that's the point of these experiments — not to have all the answers, but to keep creating spaces where we can go close to inner jyoti a little more."

items.descriptionOriginal: A curled leaf, a handful of clay and a shallow depression in the earth have become the starting point for an unusual water conservation experiment in the forests of Keonjhar district. The idea is: can children learn to hold on to water by observing how nature does it? A lesson hidden in a leaf On a walk through the dry forest slopes around Haladipani, a village in Odisha's Keonjhar district a local elder stopped beside a curled sal leaf. Inside its cupped surface, a thin film of dew had collected, holding on to moisture even as the surrounding ground dried in the heat. For the children accompanying him, it was a small observation with a larger question behind it. If a leaf could catch and retain a little water, could they recreate that ability on the ground, where water was harder to come by? The elder, known locally as the 'jungle master', encouraged them to try. Instead of using plastic sheets or manufactured containers, the children began experimenting with sal leaves and clay to make small pits that could collect and retain water. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Village Square (@villagesquareindia) The experiment was documented by Biswabijayini Mohanty in a report published by Village Square on 16 September 2026, titled A Lesson in Water Conservation from a Leaf . The report describes how an observation made during a forest walk developed into a practical exercise in water conservation, with the children learning through trial, error and close attention to their surroundings. How the children made the pits The children dug shallow depressions near the forest edge using simple tools, sticks and their hands. But they soon encountered a problem: the loose soil absorbed the water poured into the pits before it could remain there for long. The jungle master helped them rethink the design. First, they laid broad sal leaves across the bottom and sides of each depression, overlapping them like roof tiles . They then spread clay soil over the leaves, pressing and smoothing it until the hollow took the shape of a shallow bowl. The two materials served different purposes. The leaf layer helped support the clay as it dried, while the compacted clay formed a lining intended to slow the movement of water into the surrounding soil. The children repeated the process, allowing the clay to set before filling the pits. Within about two weeks, they had created a network of small water-holding depressions along the forest edges. According to Village Square, the pits were generally no deeper than a forearm and rarely wider than a large dining plate. There was no plastic lining , costly equipment or elaborate construction involved. The materials came from the landscape around them, and the method evolved through observation and experimentation. When the rains put the idea to the test The pits were intended to hold water during the dry months. But after several days of rain, runoff carried loose soil down the slopes, turning surrounding water sources muddy. The pits, however, appeared to retain relatively clearer water. According to Village Square, the pits were generally no deeper than a forearm and rarely wider than a large dining plate. Photograph: (Gadadhar Dehury-Via Village Square) The explanation lies partly in the way water behaves when it is allowed to settle. Rainwater flowing over exposed ground can carry suspended particles of soil and other sediment. When that water collects in a relatively still depression, heavier particles can gradually settle at the bottom, leaving the water above them less cloudy. The report also records visits by wildlife, including barking deer, rabbits, mongooses and squirrels, which were seen drinking from the pits. There is an important distinction, however, between water that looks clear and water that is safe to drink. The report does not provide laboratory test results establishing the potability of water collected in these pits. What science tells us about sal leaves and water The principle behind the experiment has parallels in traditional agricultural practices documented elsewhere in Odisha A study compiled by Dr Prasanta Kumar Mishra, a principal scientist at the Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture, describes how tribal farmers in Pakanagaon village in Kandhamal district use sal leaves as mulch in turmeric fields. The account, published by LEISA India, notes that farmers spread a layer approximately 20–25 cm thick over their fields before the monsoon. The leaf cover helps conserve soil moisture, reduce runoff and soil loss, suppress weeds and protect the soil from the direct impact of raindrops. Mulching works by covering the soil surface, reducing its exposure to direct sunlight and wind and helping slow evaporation. It can also reduce the force with which raindrops strike the ground, limiting the displacement of soil particles. Depending on the soil and rainfall conditions, this cover can allow more water to remain available in the soil. The Haladipani experiment uses sal leaves differently: rather than spreading them over agricultural land, the children place them beneath a compacted clay lining in small depressions. Both of these practices show how locally available sal can be used to manage moisture and soil. The children are not simply being told that water is scarce or that forests must be protected. They are being encouraged to observe a leaf, understand what it does, test an idea and learn from what happens next. It is a practical starting point for environmental learning. Sources: 'Farmers' practices of improving soil health by mulching in semi-arid india' : By Dr Prasanta Kumar Mishra 'Ground Report-A lesson in water conservation from a leaf' : By Biswabijayini Mohanty, Published on 16 September 2026

items.title: Για 60 χρόνια, οι άνθρωποι άκουγαν λάθος τον στίχο «προσποιούμαι ότι προσεύχομαι» στο «California Dreamin». Αλλάζει εντελώς το τραγούδι.
items.titleOriginal: For 60 years, people have misheard the ‘pretend to pray’ lyric in ‘California Dreamin’.’ It totally changes the song.
items.description: Το "California Dreamin'" είναι αναμφισβήτητα η πιο δημοφιλής επιτυχία των The Mamas & the Papas, που αγκάλιασαν οι hippie Boomers μετά την κυκλοφορία του το 1965 και αγαπήθηκε από γενιές έκτοτε. Υπάρχει μόνο ένα πρόβλημα με το τραγούδι: μια ολόκληρη δέσμη ακροατών έχει κάνει λάθος έναν βασικό στίχο εδώ και 60 χρόνια. Ο JB Eckl εξηγεί σε ένα βίντεο των Sacred Riffs: «Το «California Dreamin» μπορεί να είναι το…
items.descriptionOriginal: “California Dreamin'” is arguably The Mamas & the Papas’ most popular hit, embraced by hippie Boomers upon its 1965 release and beloved by generations since. There’s just one problem with the song : a whole bunch of listeners have gotten a key lyric dead wrong for 60 years. JB Eckl explains in a Sacred Riffs video : “‘California Dreamin” may be the only hit song whose central event is a fake prayer.” The lyrics describe someone stopping into a church, kneeling, and pretending to pray to get out of the cold. However, countless people have misheard the lyric “and I pretend to pray” as “and I began to pray.” Clearly, pretending to pray and beginning to pray are two very different things. So what’s the deal? View this post on Instagram The real-life story behind the ‘pretend to pray’ lyric As Eckl explains, Michelle Phillips added the church story to the song because it reflected something that had happened in real life. Phillips and her husband, John Phillips, were outside in a New York winter, and Michelle wanted to go into St. Patrick’s Cathedral. “But John wouldn’t go in because he had strong, negative feelings about religion, stemming from his parochial school childhood,” Eckl says. John presented the beginnings of the song “California Dreamin'” to Michelle, and she added the church memory to the lyrics. John reportedly hated the addition and wanted to change it, but it stuck. Eckl says he’d spent his life thinking the lyric was “I began to pray,” not “I pretend to pray.” Many people in the comments agreed, and they aren’t the only ones. Cass Elliot had the lyric wrong, too Cass Elliott, the other female band member, sang the lyric as “began” in the background vocals on the album and on tour until Michelle corrected her. “We were somewhere in the Midwest in the middle of a tour, and we were doing a sound check,” Phillips told her daughter, Chynna . “We were singing ‘California Dreamin’,’ and we get to that lyric and Cass says, ‘Oh, wait, wait, wait, wait, wait, wait. What’d you say?’ ‘I got down on my knees and pretend to pray.’ And she says, ‘That’s not the lyric.’ And I said, ‘Yeah, what do you mean? I wrote it. It is the lyric.’ She said, ‘Oh, well, I sang “I began to pray” on the record.'” So don’t feel bad if you thought it was “began.” Even a quarter of the band had it wrong for a while there. How ‘pretend to pray’ alters the meaning of the song Some people were dismayed to learn that what they thought was a lyric of devotion was actually a lyric of doubt. Eckl spends a little time exploring the verse and its meaning. “The idea of pretending to pray changes the character of the moment completely,” Eckl explains. “What is prayer if you’re not sure if you believe? People sometimes enter sacred spaces for warmth, for community, for beauty, sometimes out of desperation, and only discover later if there was anything spiritual about it.” The lyric about the preacher liking the cold because he knows it will keep people there adds another layer to the song’s narrative. Some might see it as cynical. Others might find hope in it (especially if they hear the line as “the preacher lights the coals,” which is also a common mishearing). Finally, Eckl discusses the song’s iconic alto flute solo and, surprisingly, ties it to the Persian mystic poet Rumi. “In the poetry of Rumi, the flute represents longing, spiritual homesickness,” Eckl shares. Interesting, considering “California Dreamin'” was originally written about physical homesickness. Eckl leaves listeners with food for thought: two lines from a Rumi poem speaking from the flute’s perspective: “Since I was cut from the reedbed, I have made this crying sound…anyone pulled from a source longs to go back.” Really puts “California Dreamin'” in a whole new light, doesn’t it? You can find more Sacred Riffs takes on the intersection of spirituality and rock n’ roll on JB Eckl’s Instagram . The post For 60 years, people have misheard the ‘pretend to pray’ lyric in ‘California Dreamin’.’ It totally changes the song. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Για κάποιους, η εύρεση μιας εφευρετικής αποκριάτικης στολή μπορεί να είναι ένα τεράστιο (και μερικές φορές αγχωτικό) κατόρθωμα. Γι' αυτό, τα τελευταία 12 περίπου χρόνια, πολλοί στην Ιαπωνία έχουν ντυθεί με τα πιο ξεκαρδιστικά κοσμικά κοστούμια που μπορούν να βρουν. Ονομάζεται «Jimi Halloween», με το «Jimi» να σημαίνει «απλό, απλό, συγκρατημένο, νηφάλιο», σύμφωνα με ένα διαδικτυακό ιαπωνικό λεξικό. Th…
items.descriptionOriginal: For some, finding an inventive Halloween costume can be a huge (and sometimes stressful) feat. That’s why, for the last 12 years or so, many in Japan have dressed in the most hilariously mundane costumes they can find. It’s called “Jimi Halloween, ” with “Jimi” meaning “plain, simple, subdued, sober,” according to an online Japanese dictionary . The gist is this: think of everyday situations. Perhaps someone is trying, but failing, to open a plastic bag at the supermarket for their bananas. Or maybe someone bought popcorn and a large soda at the movies but has no place to put them. The idea is that we so often find ourselves in these daily situations. The contenders for best “most boring” costumes seem to get more and more creative each year. View this post on Instagram As ‘mundane’ as possible Spoon and Tamago , a self-described “Japanese art, design and culture website,” explains that the tradition dates back to 2014. They share, “The tradition was started by a group of adults at Daily Portal Z , who kind of wanted to participate in the festivities of Halloween but were too embarrassed to go all out in witch or zombie costumes. So instead of the flashy and flamboyant costumes they had been seeing gain popularity in Japan, they decided to dress up in mundane, everyday costumes.” Under a post explaining the idea from the First Degree podcast, many share the costumes they’ve come up with over the years. One Instagrammer has an elaborate plan. “This year, I am going as ‘guy checking out at the grocery store but realizes he left his wallet in the car and has to hurry out to the parking lot to go get it.'” Another shares their winning look. “I went to the office as ‘stock photo of woman eating salad.’ (The stock photo part truly took it to the next level.) ‘Counteracting’ Halloween The Halloween “movement” has gained traction over the years. In a Reddit thread titled “The Japanese have perfected the mundane Halloween costume,” one person shares, “I just heard about this on NPR yesterday. Apparently Halloween has become really big in Tokyo and a lot of people go all out on costumes, so the last few years someone has been throwing a party to ‘counteract’ the trend. Hundreds of people come in mundane costumes that show an awkward or irritating moment in daily life. Hilarious!” Another adds a few of their favorites. “I saw some of these on twitter last(?) year, including ‘Man who doesn’t know his backpack is open’, ‘Woman whose picture is on packets of noodles’ and ‘Door attendant’. I love that ‘person who only has Nike shoes’ is otherwise head-to-not-quite-foot Adidas.” 7 funny Jimi Halloween costumes 1. The man who opened up a Coke bottle that had already been shaken. View this post on Instagram 2. The woman who accidentally “missed trash day.” View this post on Instagram 3. Photo “assistant” whose job is to “make kids laugh. View this post on Instagram 4. The guy who gets too many sauces for his meal. View this post on Instagram 5. “Person listening to the song they’re about to sing next at Karaoke” Photo Credit: @YSSkywalker , Spoon & Tamago 6. Person who tries to drink coffee, but forgets they’re wearing a mask. Photo credit: Japanagram 7. The guy who smiles at every dog who walks by. Photo credit: @YSSkywalker , Spoon & Tomago The post Japan’s ‘jimi’ Halloween costumes are meant to appear ‘mundane.’ They’re actually brilliant. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Overwhelmed by all the ‘sentimental’ objects you’re saving? A new study reveals a better way.

Μαζί με όλα τα σκουπίδια, πολλοί ενήλικες σήμερα έχουν κληρονομήσει την ιδέα ότι πρέπει να αποθηκεύουν και να αγαπούν συναισθηματικά αντικείμενα. Θα έπρεπε…
items.descriptionOriginal: Millennials and Gen Xers often hate clutter . It’s a natural reaction to being raised by Baby Boomer parents who loved collecting tchotchkes, antiques, fine china, and crystal sets they only used on the rarest occasions. Along with all the junk, many adults today have inherited the idea that they must save and cherish sentimental items. They should be packed away, as they’re too precious for everyday use, and kept for…well, forever. A new scientific study is challenging that notion in a big way. Study says we feel more connected to objects that we use, not save Research by Dan Grossman and colleagues in the Journal of Consumer Psychology set out to measure sentimental value and, crucially, see how it can change over time. In a series of studies, Grossman tracked people’s use of and feelings about objects that held deep meaning for them, even simple ones. In one study, Psychology Today reported that 214 university students decorated a keychain with words related to a favorite memory. One group was instructed to set the keychain aside for the duration of the experiment, about two weeks. The other group used it daily. In the end, students who used the keychain regularly felt a stronger connection to it. Its sentimental value had increased through regular use and contact rather than being tucked away somewhere. In a Psychology Today article, Janina Steinmetz, Ph.D ., writes, “The researchers propose that using these objects strengthens the connection between the object and its associated memories by allowing the memories to come up more frequently, by reminding us why these memories matter to us, and by strengthening the connection to our identity.” Research gives overwhelmed adults much-needed permission Clutter has become a huge problem for many Americans. In fact, over half of American adults report feeling “overwhelmed” by the amount of physical possessions they have, according to the BBC . It’s gotten so bad that self-storage use has skyrocketed in recent years. The Wall Street Journal reports that the “craze has reached a tipping point.” About a third of Americans have so much stuff that they need a separate unit outside their home to house it all. Professional declutterer Bev Hitchins told the BBC, “People gather stuff to protect themselves. It’s an illusion, though. It doesn’t make them happy—it’s a cover-up. We get so busy maintaining stuff, keeping it, making sure there’s a place for it. It’s not greed. It’s trying to fill up a hole that’s so big it will never be filled.” Most people have no idea what to do with all of the stuff that they’ve accumulated. In addition to the things that are hard to get rid of for logistical reasons (old paint, mattresses, dead batteries), there’s the deluge of sentimental keepsakes. Children’s artwork, items from our own childhood, the crystal dining set you inherited from your parents. Crushing guilt, rather than fondness, keeps us anchored to many of these things. The new research opens up a wonderful new possibility: use it if you can, and consider ditching everything but a handful of real keepers. Scientists now suggest that using that fine china regularly will likely help you feel a stronger connection to your parents and grandparents, rather than storing it in a massive cabinet where it gathers dust. And that souvenir mug from a family vacation? Use it or lose it. At the very least, keep the important things handy. Southern Living writes that if you can’t access something within 10 minutes, if it lives in a storage unit miles away, how important can it really be? Yes, these cherished items might break or finally wear out when you use or handle them a lot, but the daily connection to those memories well outweighs the risk. After all, the memories and stories will last forever, even when the physical items surely will not. The post Overwhelmed by all the ‘sentimental’ objects you’re saving? A new study reveals a better way. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Vincent van Gogh’s Starry Night has been capturing the public’s imagination for over 100 years. From swirling deep blues to glowing yellow stars, the emotion behind every brushstroke leaps off the canvas. It is easily one of the most-discussed paintings in human history. Millions of people travel from around the world just to catch a glimpse of it hanging on the wall at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City. Art historians assumed the iconic scene was purely a work of passionate creativity. Considering Van Gogh’s history of mental health issues, it’s easy to chalk up those swirling vortexes to reflections of his inner struggle. After all, the artist loved capturing a setting’s emotions, not its stark reality. But modern science keeps revealing deeper secrets hidden within the layers of paint. South Korean researchers now suggest something that could rewrite our understanding of Starry Night . The swirling nocturnal sky might actually have been the start of a new day. A century-old timeline gets a surprising update Art historians long believed the masterpiece was painted in mid-June of 1889. Van Gogh was staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence at the time. Letters he penned that summer stated he was working hard in his studio. So the mid-June timeline for the work held, until a group of South Korean researchers recently called it into question . Their findings, outlined in Scientific Reports , test old assumptions against meteorological and astronomical data. The group delved into star charts and local weather logs from late-19th-century France. Seeking data points that matched the scene in Starry Night , they systematically cross-referenced every detail. They even dug through Van Gogh’s personal family letters for any additional clues. Van Gogh wrote as often as he could to his beloved brother, Theo. He treated his letters like a journal, detailing his daily life, painting progress, and his immediate natural surroundings. In one crucial letter, he mentioned to Theo a specific detail about the local wildlife. He wrote about cicadas singing loudly in the warm morning air. He noted how their loud buzzing filled the countryside. That small observation about the insect became a massive clue. The buzz that unlocked the mystery Cicadas do not sing at just any time of the year. Their noisy chorus heavily depends on warm weather and seasonal shifts. In Southern France, they only emerge and sing during specific summer temperature peaks. Mid-June was simply too early for that level of cicada activity in the region. By combining the insect timing with precise celestial positioning, the research team made a huge breakthrough. They mapped out the exact alignment of the moon, planets, and stars above the asylum. This celestial map pointed away from June entirely. Instead, it matched a specific dawn sky that appeared around July 22, 1889. This discovery completely shifts our understanding of the legendary artwork. It was not just a wild dream painted in total darkness. It was a precise, breathtaking observation of an actual early summer morning with cicadas buzzing in the background. The research suggests that Van Gogh painted the night light fading into day. He combined elements of stars burning bright against the morning blue. He took that real moment in the sky and turned it into everlasting artistry. The post What day was ‘Starry Night’? A hidden clue in Van Gogh’s letters may unlock a 130-year-old mystery appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article kicks off The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. It was winter break, and Dilan Mehta had time on his hands. His dad was packing for a mission trip to Kenya, where he’d been volunteering with Kenya Relief , a medical organization that runs a school in Migori, for years. Dilan packed a bag of stuffed animals for the children there. Then he glanced at his 3D printer. He started designing LEGO-inspired sets, printing each one out, and tucking them in alongside the stuffed animals. Somewhere between one print and the next, a different thought took shape. The school had students who could use a curriculum, and his dad had room in a suitcase. That’s how a 3D printer ended up in Migori, Kenya, and why it’s still being used to teach students today. What is Student Makers? Student Makers is a nonprofit that offers free STEM workshops to students across the United States, Kenya, and India, and every instructor is a former student. Most of them are still in high school. The organization was founded in California in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior. There was no space at his school where students interested in technology and making could come together to learn, so he built one. He called it the Maker Hub Club Initiative, secured a $5,000 grant from a social impact scholarship, and got it off the ground. The framework was three steps: learn a skill , make a project, showcase it. He was in his first year of college when he started handing it off. Serve: the fourth pillar Dilan didn’t find Student Makers; rather, Anthony found him. Roughly six years ago, Dilan was only in 8th grade and had entered an Autodesk design contest with a 3D-printed fingerboard, one that used flexible filament on the grip surface to behave like rubber. Anthony came across it and reached out. Would Dilan want to join a group where students build things and learn from each other? He joined, took the 3D printing course, came back as an instructor, and eventually rebuilt the entire curriculum from scratch around design thinking rather than output. A few years later, he was running the organization. But he felt that the project’s mission needed some rethinking. The original framework had three steps: learn, make, showcase. Dilan added a fourth, serve, because the workshops were primarily reaching students who already had resources, and that wasn’t what he’d signed up for. His dad’s Kenya-bound suitcase gave him the opening for a bigger idea to launch. Teaching through rain and static When Dilan sent that 3D printer to Kenya Relief Academy, he wasn’t thinking about it as a program. He was thinking about a school with 800 students, roughly 170 to 190 of them orphaned children, consistently ranked the top primary school in its region out of more than 800, and without any STEM infrastructure. His dad’s Kenya Relief contacts connected him to the teachers there, and he started meeting with them remotely three times a week. Every session ran over video call, Dilan in the US and the teachers in Migori, and when the Wi-Fi dropped, which it often would, they’d wait, reconnect, and keep going. He trained them in Autodesk Fusion 360, Tinkercad, and 3D printer operation, working through how to teach all of it to a classroom he’s never seen in person. “They constantly have Wi-Fi issues,” Dilan said. “Anytime there’s rain, they basically lose connection. Just being patient, being empathetic , understanding that that’s just the situation.” Ruth Agongo, a teacher at Kenya Relief Academy, described what it looked like from the other end. “You are a game-changer,” she said. “Whatever you have taught us, we are putting into action because the kids are really excited by the technology.” Jacob A few semesters into his time at Georgia Tech, once Dilan had actually taken a step back from Student Makers and was serving mostly as an advisory board member, Dilan got a message from the teachers at Kenya Relief Academy. They needed help with a science fair project: an Arduino-based robot that could navigate a garden, measure soil moisture at different points, and decide where to water. Dilan didn’t know much about robotics, but he was at Georgia Tech, so he asked around. Twelve students from the university ended up on the project. They built components in Atlanta while the Kenya team built in Migori, troubleshot over video call, and sent physical supplies through a similar suitcase network that had carried the original printer. That team placed third at regionals of the Kenya Science and Engineering Fair. One of the students on it, a ninth-grader named Jacob, now leads Kenya Relief Academy’s robotics team. His dream is to become a rocket engineer at NASA. A family connection in India Rohan Naegle, who led Student Makers before the current team took over, brought a similar program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, after his grandfather put him in touch with the school. Live 3D printing classes run there over video call, using the same structure. More than 25 secondary students have completed the program, and a donated printer stays at the school. Both the Kenya and India connections came organically, through family. How the pipeline runs Aarush Goel, who now leads the high school chapters, came in the same way Dilan did: a friend pulled him in to co-teach a Python workshop, and he showed up not entirely sure what he was doing. “You just start teaching and everything goes into place,” he said. He’s since led five workshop tracks across the US, and next year he’ll start a Student Makers chapter at his own college. Instructors are recruited the same way at every level. At the end of each cycle, a call goes out for anyone who wants to come back and teach the next round. Usually one or two students say yes. They already know the program from the inside, which tends to make them good at the part that matters most: building something new students actually want to stay in. Anthony, watching from his current advisory role, put it plainly. “It’s more relatable, a high schooler showing a middle schooler how to do some 3D printing than someone who’s already a young adult,” he said. “So it’s nice keeping that peer-to-peer instruction model.” He’s 25. The organization he started as a high school senior just turned seven. Growing the network Student Makers recently joined a partnership with Youth Technology Corps Global Alliance , a network of schools across roughly 12 countries that has been running a similar peer-learning model since 1998. YTC has been doing this for nearly three decades and has school connections worldwide; Student Makers brings the volunteers and the curriculum. This fall, programs are launching under the partnership in Mexico, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Illinois, with the 3D printing and CAD curriculum going into Mexico specifically. “I would have never imagined that we would have this extensive of a reach,” Anthony said. The reach he couldn’t have imagined started with a simple observation: students interested in technology and making didn’t have a space to come together. So he built one. Why Student Makers opens this year’s series Each year, The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers series runs in the weeks before Thanksgiving, and this year, for the first time, every person in it is 30 or under. When Aarush reached out to us with the Student Makers story last summer, we spent weeks talking with the people who built this organization and were honestly floored by their dedication, hard work, and willingness to serve others. The five other changemakers in this year’s series were nominated by The Optimist Daily community, but Student Makers was not. It was the story that inspired the decision behind this year’s “30 and under” theme. This article skims the surface of the deeper story behind Student Makers. If you want to learn more about their incredible work, hang tight for a podcast episode featuring the voices behind this initiative. It’ll be coming out in early 2027. In the meantime, you can learn more and support their work at www.studentmakers.org . The post Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most social programs ask you to declare yourself before they’ll give you anything. You fill out a form, check a box, explain your circumstances to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built All The Same Organization around the idea that this moment, identifying yourself as someone who needs help, was what kept people from asking at all. Vivian lives in Cedar Park, Texas, but the organization operates nationally. She is, remarkably, only 17 years old. ATS delivers supply packages directly to low-income families through Title I schools: food, hygiene products, household necessities, school supplies. Families request what they need through an anonymous sign-up system. No one who receives support is required to name themselves as the recipient. “Just because resources exist does not mean that it’s accessible,” wrote Anika Luangaphay, who co-founded ATS alongside Vivian. The anonymous system, Luangaphay explained, was designed to let families “choose what type of support they want” without attaching their identity to the request. Volunteers with the All The Same Organization Reaching Title I families across the country Since its founding, ATS has grown to more than 200 chapters with roughly 8,000 volunteers and has distributed over 150,000 supplies to families at Title I schools. In a single back-to-school season , the organization served five schools and delivered more than 15,000 school supplies. Vendor events in the Austin and Cedar Park area have raised more than $75,000 in goods. ATS brings supplies directly to schools, removing the need for families to travel. Outreach is conducted across language barriers so that immigrant families can find and navigate the program without information being another wall to get over. Aoto Yamazaki, a longtime volunteer, described Vivian’s approach as incredibly empathetic and well-thought-out: “What makes Vivian’s work especially meaningful to me is how intentionally she considers each student’s culture due to her past experiences as an immigrant.” Cultural Surprises Cultural Surprises works like this: volunteers research the cultural background of a recipient family, then create handmade arts and crafts based on what they find. The crafts go out alongside the supply packages. More than 500 crafts have been made for over 60 recipients. Volunteers don’t just pack boxes; they do the work to understand the people they’re packing for. Yamazaki wrote that the program had changed what he understood about volunteering: “Being part of this work has taught me so much about cultures I previously knew little about, including Hmong culture.” Luangaphay connected it directly to Vivian’s own history. “She had told me herself that she grew up suppressing her culture due to being a Vietnamese immigrant,” Luangaphay wrote, “so now she recognizes the students in Title I schools often neglect their own culture, too.” The crafts are partly a way of giving back something that growing up between cultures tends to cost. ATS has now secured funding for a Cultural Spotlight Scholarship. Rather than asking volunteers to make crafts for recipients, this program invites students to create art and crafts inspired by their own cultures, with a short written description of what the piece means and where it comes from. Those descriptions get shared with a wider audience. Winners will receive $1,250. The goal, as Luangaphay described it, is to give participants “a deep dive into a culture, whether it’s their own or another person’s.” A classroom, and what came after After noticing a gap in career exposure at the schools she worked with, Vivian fundraised for medical supplies, including mannequins, suture kits, and stethoscopes, then developed a partnership with Age of Central Texas to build a functional medical classroom at Dobie Middle School. When the school went through a turnaround and that classroom was shut down, she turned her attention to other Title I schools rather than walking away. “Her willingness to keep finding ways to help, even when her original efforts did not go as planned, is something that has always stayed with me,” Yamazaki wrote. Yamazaki saw the same thing in smaller moments. Early in his time with the organization, he told Vivian he wanted to start his own project after being inspired by her work. “She selflessly gave me her time, advice, and guidance, walking me through how to turn my ideas into something that could create a real impact,” he wrote. She was, at that point, a teenager running a multi-chapter national nonprofit. Vivian received two nominations for this series: one from her co-founder and one from a volunteer she inspired to build something of his own. Both of them described an organization built on one idea: that people should be able to ask for help without giving anything of themselves away to get it. Learn more and get involved at www.allthesame.org . Vivian Ho, founder.
