Πολλές από αυτές τις πόλεις r…
items.descriptionOriginal: From the deep South to colonial New England, certain U.S. locales have developed chilling reputations for reports of apparitions and other paranormal activity. Long shadows have been cast by histories steeped in calamity, and stories abound of restless souls condemned to cemeteries and peevish poltergeists with bones to pick. Many of these cities relish their notoriety, with multiple laying claim to the title of most haunted in the country. We detail a few of them below, but whether you use this list as a roster of places you dare not enter or as a resource for your next vacation, proceed with caution: We can’t promise that reading our roundup won’t summon the spirits mentioned within it. Savannah, Georgia Glen Richard—iStock/Getty Images Plus Savannah offers all the charm of the South and all the unease of a Southern Gothic novel — if you know where to look. Lurking amid the oak-lined streets and majestic mansions are specters borne of centuries of tragedy (or so the story goes). Founded in 1733, the city played major roles in the Revolutionary and Civil Wars and was ravaged by several yellow fever outbreaks in the 1800s. The souls lost in those events are said to haunt Savannah’s historic cemeteries and buildings. “Visitors and locals alike report unexplained phenomena across Savannah: sudden cold spots, shadow figures, voices, apparitions, and objects moving without cause,” claims local hotel Bellwether House, which was built in 1876. “Ghost sightings aren’t confined to one building — they’re woven into the city itself.” Even its own chamber of commerce boasts its reputation as “the most haunted city in America” (a title New Orleans also claims). Check out 10 of the spookiest places in Savannah. Atchison, Kansas DonsESLAdventure—iStock Editorial/Getty Images Plus Known for being the birthplace of Amelia Earhart , Atchison’s other claim to fame is its purported paranormal activity. Situated on the Missouri River, it’s home to the infamous Sallie House . Legend has it that after a young girl named Sallie died there during a failed appendicitis operation in 1905, her ghost stuck around. Though locals had long considered the abode haunted, the story truly took hold in 1993 when a couple moved in and began experiencing ominous phenomena — including a fire, objects moving around on their own, and unexplained scratches. Other eerie sites in Atchison (called “America’s most haunted town” by its tourism department) include the McInteer Villa , an 1889 Victorian mansion that’s elicited reports of supernatural occurrences; the Rose Trunk Building , where visitors have claimed they sensed an unseen presence; and Benedictine College, said to be haunted by the spirits of monks who founded it over 150 years ago. New Orleans, Louisiana lightphoto—iStock/Getty Images Plus Welcome to New Orleans, a 308-year-old city rife with historical trauma. Its early days were marked by violence and sorrow, which continued into the 19th century as slavery, the Civil War, and several disease outbreaks took their toll. A merging of West African spiritual practices and Catholicism gave rise to its distinct voodoo tradition , and today, “the line between the living and the dead often feels surprisingly thin,” per the city’s tourism department. If you’re looking for a hair-raising time, you should certainly visit the French Quarter. Book a stay at the Andrew Jackson Hotel — believed to be haunted by five boys who perished there in a fire when it was a boarding school — or dine at Antoine’s Restaurant, reportedly home to 19th-century spirits who peer out from the bathroom mirrors. The ghost of author William Faulkner is said to remain in the rooms he rented in the neighborhood, which have since been converted into a bookstore called Faulkner House Books. Learn about more haunted places in New Orleans. Salem, Massachusetts AndTheyTravel—iStock Editorial / Getty Images Plus Salem’s dark history has seemingly cast a spell over the colonial New England town. The area’s notorious witch trials saw around 200 people accused of witchcraft in the 1690s. About 30 were found guilty and at least 19 were put to death. Today, this chilling past resurfaces in reports of ghost sightings and other supernatural phenomena. Proctor’s Ledge , the trials’ primary execution site, is said to be haunted, with visitors reporting cold spots, incandescent orbs, and a disembodied voice, per Ghost City Tours. The Joshua Ward House , built on the site where George Corwin — High Sheriff during the witch trials — once lived, is also the stuff of legend: An accused man named Giles Corey is rumored to have cursed Corwin and the town of Salem with his final breath during his execution. At the Old Burying Point Cemetery , established in 1637, condemned souls are believed to be responsible for mysterious shadows, noises, mist, and an overwhelming sense of despair. Anoka, Minnesota Officially known as “the Halloween Capital of the World,” Anoka is rich with tales of the paranormal. Reportedly haunted buildings include the Anoka State Hospital , a psychiatric institution that opened in 1900; Colonial Hall, where furniture is said to move around inexplicably after dark; and the old Anoka library, with a known history of “books flying off of shelves,” per local outlet HometownSource. The Anoka County Historical Society, which formerly used the library as its headquarters, offers guided ghost tours that are “60% history, 40% folklore” and based on real stories from the people who live and work in the city’s buildings. Virginia City, Nevada NNehring—E+/Getty Images “To say everything is haunted in this old mining town is not too far from the truth,” proclaims Virginia City’s tourism department. The locale topped the ranking in the 2026 Spookiest Cities Report , a playful analysis by home security company Vivint. The ranking used seven measures, adjusted for population: haunted places, ghost sightings, funeral services, haunted houses, psychics and astrologers, spiritual shops, and spooky Google search volume. Visitors can explore eerie places like the Gold Hill Hotel, Nevada’s oldest, where rumors persist of children’s ghosts running the halls, or bring home a bottle of Cemetery Gin, the city’s own distilled spirit. This month — dubbed Hauntober — one of the area’s top ghost experts is leading paranormal investigations at the historic St. Mary’s Art Center, which was originally a hospital and is known as one of Virginia City’s most haunted buildings. Gettysburg, Pennsylvania pabradyphoto— iStock/Getty Images Plus The Civil War’s Battle of Gettysburg in 1863 resulted in over 50,000 casualties, and many believe that the spirits of the soldiers who died on the battlefield remain there, reliving the brutal conflict. For over 100 years, visitors and locals have reported “phantom footsteps, ghostly drumbeats, and echoes of musket fire and cannon blasts,” per History . Other spots in the city, widely known as one of the country’s most haunted places , have their own eerie history tied to the war. The Jennie Wade House Museum commemorates, and is said to be possessed by, the only civilian killed in the battle. Visitors have claimed to hear whispers, feel cold spots, and see Wade’s ghost floating through the rooms. Those daring enough to walk into the Sachs Covered Bridge — where a trio of Confederate soldiers were executed for impersonating Union troops — may encounter three disembodied heads or feel phantom fingers tapping their shoulders.

items.title: Η Πολωνέζα που μετέφερε λαθραία 2.500 εβραϊκά παιδιά σε εργαλειοθήκες, βαλίτσες και φέρετρα απέρριψε την ετικέτα «ήρωας» του Β' Παγκοσμίου Πολέμου
items.titleOriginal: Polish woman who smuggled 2,500 Jewish children to safety in toolboxes, suitcases, and coffins rejected WWII ‘hero’ label
items.description: Ο πατέρας της Irena Sendler της δίδαξε ότι αν κάποιος πνίγεται, τον βοηθάς, ανεξάρτητα από τη θρησκεία ή την εθνικότητα του. Αυτή η ανατροφή οδήγησε την Πολωνή Καθολική κοινωνική λειτουργό να ρισκάρει τη ζωή της για να βοηθήσει να σωθούν 2.500 μωρά και παιδιά Εβραίων από τα νύχια του ναζιστικού τρόμου. Ο Sendler ήταν ένας 29χρονος κοινωνικός λειτουργός στη Βαρσοβία όταν ξεκίνησε ο Β' Παγκόσμιος Πόλεμος…
items.descriptionOriginal: Irena Sendler’s father taught her that if someone is drowning, you help them, regardless of their religion or nationality. That upbringing led the Polish Catholic social worker to risk her own life to help save 2,500 Jewish babies and children from the clutches of Nazi terror. Sendler was a 29-year-old social worker in Warsaw when World War II began in 1939. The following year, the Nazis forced Warsaw’s Jews into the ghetto, and Sendler began using her position and connections to smuggle food and money to them. She joined Zegota, the underground, state-sponsored Council for Aid to Jews, which formed in 1942. Zegota helped hide Polish Jews from Hitler’s regime, in addition to providing them with food, financial assistance, forged documents, and medical care. As head of Zegota’s children’s section in 1943, Sendler focused her efforts on getting babies and children to safety. View this post on Instagram How she got into the Warsaw ghetto to help Between 1940 and 1943, most of the Jews in the Warsaw ghetto were killed. Tens of thousands died of starvation and disease in the dirty, overcrowded conditions. Around 265,000 were sent to the Treblinka extermination camp in 1942. An uprising of resistors resulted in the destruction of what remained of the ghetto and the deportation of whoever was left in May of 1943. In the midst of all of that chaos and killing, Irena Sendler and her companions focused on smuggling babies and children out of the Warsaw ghetto. Sendler entered the ghetto to help by obtaining a pass to monitor health conditions. “German authorities were afraid of being exposed to deadly diseases like typhus and tuberculosis,” historian Dr. Ewa Wampuszyc shares in a video interview . “These were diseases that were actually caused by the ghettos that they themselves had created.” Ironically, that fear allowed Zegota helpers like Sendler to get into the highly guarded ghetto prison. The Nazis thought Sendler was helping control and monitor disease epidemics. Really, she was providing aid to the Jews in whatever way she could, even creating a network of other workers with passes to help. Smuggling out the Jewish children Sendler connected with Jewish welfare activists in the ghetto to identify children and families to help, explains Dr. Wampuszyc . However, families did not always agree on whether to send their children with Sendler and her helpers. In hindsight, it’s clear that Sendler’s smuggling network was their best chance for survival. In real time, however, those decisions were brutal. “When my friend and I were going to the ghetto to pick up those children, there were hellish scenes,” Sendler shared in an interview later in life. “A mother wanted her child to go, while the father did not. A grandmother wanted to hand over a child; a mama didn’t. They asked for a guarantee. What kind of a guarantee could I give them? I could not even guarantee that I would get past the sentry. So when I went to a Jewish family for a child, I could not guarantee that the child would live.” Sendler and her companions smuggled kids out in suitcases, sacks, ambulances, and coffins. One baby escaped the ghetto in a toolbox. The children were often hidden in plain sight in convents, orphanages, or with foster families under Polish children’s names. Sendler kept meticulous records in hopes the children might reunite with their families. The Jewish and Polish names of each child and their location were written on strips of paper, stored in milk jars, and buried in the backyard of one of her co-conspirators for safekeeping. She endured interrogation, torture, and a death sentence, but never caved It would be remarkable for Sendler to have done all of this right under the Nazis’ noses and never get caught. What’s even more remarkable is what she did when she did get caught. On October 20, 1943, the Gestapo arrested Sendler at her home after beating another woman into revealing Sendler’s name. They then took her to Pawiak prison, where they broke her legs and feet. “They beat me. Tortured me. Hence, you know, my bad legs,” she shared . “And very quickly, I got a death sentence.” Yet through it all, Sendler never revealed the children’s whereabouts. Thankfully, Zegota managed to bribe officials into releasing her before her execution. Authorities knocked her unconscious and left her by the roadside. After the war, Sendler handed the jars containing 2,500 children’s names and whereabouts over to Jewish representatives. Tragically, they found that nearly all of the children’s families had perished. She didn’t want to be called a hero Sendler was objectively a hero by every measure, but she flatly rejected the title. “Every child saved with my help is justification of my existence on this Earth, and not a title to glory,” she wrote in a 2007 letter to the Polish Senate. “The term ‘hero’ irritates me greatly,” she said in an interview. “The opposite is true. I continue to have pangs of conscience that I did so little.” Sendler died in 2008 at the age of 98. The following year, her story was made into a Hallmark television film, The Courageous Heart of Irena Sendler , with Anna Paquin starring as Sendler. The post Polish woman who smuggled 2,500 Jewish children to safety in toolboxes, suitcases, and coffins rejected WWII ‘hero’ label appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Στη δεκαετία του ’70, οι επιστήμονες είχαν μια συνάντηση με ένα φτιαγμένο φάντασμα. Σοκαρίστηκαν όταν «μίλησε» πίσω.
items.titleOriginal: In the ’70s, scientists had a séance with a made-up ghost. They were shocked when it ‘talked’ back.
items.description: Στη δεκαετία του 1970, το φάντασμα του Philip Aylseford, Άρχοντα του Diddington Manor, έγινε γνωστό. Το συντετριμμένο και θλιμμένο πνεύμα απάντησε σε ερωτήσεις σχετικά με την προηγούμενη ζωή του χτυπώντας ένα τραπέζι —μία για το «ναι» και δύο για το «όχι»—και ακόμη και γλιστρώντας το στο δωμάτιο. Το μόνο πρόβλημα είναι: ο Φίλιππος ήταν εντελώς μακιγιαρισμένος. Το 1972, ο μαθηματικός Dr. A…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the 1970s, the ghost of Philip Aylseford , Lord of Diddington Manor, made himself known. The heartbroken and grief-stricken spirit answered questions about his former life by knocking on a table —once for “yes” and twice for “no”—and even sliding it around the room. The only problem is: Philip was completely made up. In 1972, mathematician Dr. A.R.G. Owen teamed up with psychologist Dr. Joel Whitton to see if collective consciousness and human will could create paranormal phenomena. In particular, they wondered whether these elements could conjure an apparition (a ghost becoming visible). The two doctors recruited eight participants: a heating engineer, several engineering students, an accountant, and a bookkeeper. Once assembled, this technically minded cohort began carving out a backstory for Philip, which they would then memorize in every detail. The tragic, made-up tale of Philip Aylseford Depiction of Diddington Manor. Photo credit: Canva They decided he was an aristocrat, born in England in 1624, a Catholic, and a close friend of Charles II, for whom he became a spy. Philip was, sadly, in a loveless marriage with a woman named Dorothea, the eldest daughter of a wealthy land baron. They lived together at Philip’s family estate, Diddington Manor. Philip secretly carried out an affair with a Romani woman named Margo. When Dorethea found out, she accused Margo of witchcraft. To make matters worse, Philip did nothing to defend Margo to protect his own reputation. She went to trial, was found guilty, and burned at the stake. Upon hearing the news, Philip jumped from the top of Diddington Manor, ending his fictional life at 30 years old. The classically tragic backstory was done; now it was time to try to communicate with poor dear Philip. Making first contact with a fake ghost A séance. Photo credit: Canva In the first year, the group held weekly non-traditional séances in a well-lit room without a medium. During these informal “sittings,” the group would discuss Philip’s escapades while attempting to visualize their “collective hallucination” in more detail. While some occasionally felt a presence, Philip gave no real evidence of his existence. Then the group opted for a different strategy: recreating standard Victorian spiritualist fanfare. They dimmed the lights, sang songs from the 1600s that Philip might recognize, and surrounded themselves with period objects and sketches of what they imagined Philip’s home looked like. This time, it “worked.” Philip made a knocking sound on the table. Soon, the group used this knocking mechanism to get Philip to answer questions. Apparently, he quickly knocked once when asked if he liked alcohol. When asked if he loved Dorothea, he knocked twice. In subsequent sessions, the “spirit” of Philip even seemed to exhibit a personality, as shown by how enthusiastic or hesitant his knocking was. Eventually, he slid the table from side to side, made it vibrate, and made it “dance” on one leg. Not bad for the ghost of someone who never even existed. However, Philip did have his limitations—which, conveniently, seemed to match the limitations of those who communicated with him. He could only answer questions accurately about his own life and time period, which the group already knew (since…again, they’re the ones who made it up). This implied the group’s subconscious shaped the responses. Still, some participants noted hearing whispers. It’s worth noting that Owen and Whitton’s group never did manage to get Philip to apparate. What we really learned from the Philip Experiment In the following years , the experiment would expand to other fictional ghosts— Lilith, Sebastian, Skippy, Axel, and Humphrey —each of whom yielded similar results but were ultimately deemed inconclusive. And while the Philip experiment would become the subject of a 1974 documentary and influence horror films like The Apparition (2012) and The Quiet Ones (2014), the novelty did eventually wear off, and, much like a ghost, Philip faded into obscurity. Still, Owen seemed to believe the experiment proved his theory about the power of the human mind. In a 1977 publication of The Journal of Borderland Research , he wrote: “Although members of the group speak directly to Philip and more or less treat him as a real person, he’s actually just an imaginary device for focusing the group’s mental energy. This focused energy generates what we believe are legitimate and repeatable examples of psychokinesis – or moving matter with the mind.” Other skeptics have attributed Philip’s supernatural ability to the ideomotor effect . This is where the brain subconsciously triggers the muscles to move. It’s the same mechanism that could explain how an Ouija board seems to move on its own. Or…there’s the theory that those folks actually did contact the other side. And that entity may or may not have just been assuming the role of Philip. If nothing else, our dear, troubled Philip did indeed prove that the human mind has the power to create experiences that feel remarkably real, even when the story behind them is entirely imagined. The post In the ’70s, scientists had a séance with a made-up ghost. They were shocked when it ‘talked’ back. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένα από τα πιο αξιομνημόνευτα τραγούδια των Bee Gees ξεκίνησε ως επιτυχία διασκευής από άλλο γκρουπ
items.titleOriginal: One of the Bee Gees’ most memorable songs began as a hit cover song by another group
items.description: Σύμφωνα με την κατάταξη του Spotify, το «More Than a Woman» είναι το τρίτο πιο δημοφιλές τραγούδι των Bee Gees, με σχεδόν ένα δισεκατομμύριο παιξίματα, αμέσως μετά τα «Stayin’ Alive» και «How Deep Is Your Love». Το αστείο είναι ότι όταν το ηχογράφησαν αρχικά το 1977 για το soundtrack του Saturday Night Fever, δεν το κυκλοφόρησαν καν ως single. Το 1977, ο Stevie Wond…
items.descriptionOriginal: According to Spotify rankings , “More Than a Woman” is the third most popular song by the Bee Gees , with nearly a billion plays, right after “Stayin’ Alive” and “How Deep Is Your Love.” The funny thing is, when they originally recorded it in 1977 for the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack, they didn’t even release it as a single. In 1977, Stevie Wonder’s music was meant to be featured in the film Saturday Night Fever , starring John Travolta as a Brooklynite “going nowhere” who works in a paint shop and spends his weekends competing for trophies and women on New York City dance floors. The Bee Gees take over the ‘Saturday Night Fever’ soundtrack Producer Robert Stigwood couldn’t secure the rights to Wonder’s music, so during post-production he called on the Bee Gees, a band he had managed since 1967 . The Bee Gees had traditionally been a soft rock group with folk and country roots. Still, after their 1975 hit “Jive Talkin’,” the band began exploring more rhythmic sounds, and singer Barry Gibb started experimenting with a falsetto voice popular among Black singers of the era. This kicked off a marathon writing session where, over a weekend, Barry, Maurice, and Robin Gibb wrote “Night Fever,” “Stayin’ Alive,” “More Than a Woman,” “How Deep Is Your Love,” and “If I Can’t Have You.” Talk about being in touch with the muse. “These songs were gold dust. I can’t think of any other composers you could have asked that of and had them come back with that, having not read the script,” Bill Oakes, the producer who won a Grammy for the soundtrack to the film, said in 2020 . Just as the band gave “If I Can’t Have You” to Yvonne Ellerman, they handed Tavares their demo of “More Than A Woman” to record for the film. Tavares’ core lineup was five brothers, best known for their hits “Heaven Must Be Missing an Angel” (1976) and “It Only Takes a Minute” (1975). Later, producers decided they wanted two versions of the song for the film, so the Bee Gees dusted off their demo and finished it in time for the film’s premiere. ‘More Than a Woman’ played a pivotal role in the film The Tavares version plays when Tony Manero (Travolta) practices dancing with Stephanie Mangano (Karen Lynn Gorney) for the upcoming 2001 Odyssey disco dance competition. “More Than a Woman” is a love song about a man who realizes he’s developed romantic feelings for a woman he once saw as a friend. The song features Barry’s iconic falsetto, lush harmonies, and a disco groove driven by Dennis Bryon’s drums. The Bee Gees version plays when Tony and Stephanie hit the dance floor on the big night of the disco dance competition. Saturday Night Fever was a critical and financial success, and its soundtrack became one of the highest-selling albums ever, with over 40 million copies sold. “More Than A Woman” would reach number 32 on the U.S. charts. The Tavares family is still performing, with two surviving brothers touring with the next generation to keep the group’s signature R&B sound alive. The Bee Gees’ historic career ended when Maurice passed away in 2003 at 53. Robin would follow in 2012 at 62. Barry is the band’s last surviving member. Last year, Barry sat down with Upworthy to talk about his brothers’ early years and their love for Bob Dylan . The post One of the Bee Gees’ most memorable songs began as a hit cover song by another group appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι ψυχολόγοι λένε ότι το να ευχαριστείς τους ανθρώπους έχει στην πραγματικότητα 5 κρυμμένα πλεονεκτήματα
items.titleOriginal: Psychologists say being a people pleaser actually has 5 hidden strengths
items.description: Το να είσαι ευχάριστος στους ανθρώπους συχνά συνοδεύεται από μια αρνητική ταμπέλα. Ενώ οι άνθρωποι που ευχαριστούν τείνουν να εγκαταλείπουν τις επιθυμίες και τις ανάγκες τους για τους άλλους (όπως να λένε ναι όταν θέλουν να πουν όχι), έχουν επίσης πολλές δυνάμεις και κοινωνικές δεξιότητες που τους κάνουν να ξεχωρίζουν. «Το να ευχαριστείς τους ανθρώπους δεν είναι ελάττωμα προσωπικότητας ή αδυναμία», δήλωσε ο Δρ Gary Dillon, PhD, αδειούχος ψυχολόγος…
items.descriptionOriginal: Being a people pleaser often comes with a negative label. While people pleasers tend to abandon their wants and needs for others (such as saying yes when they want to say no), they also have many strengths and social skills that set them apart. “People pleasing is not a personality flaw or a weakness,” Dr. Gary Dillon, PhD, a licensed psychologist and founder of Ally Psychological Therapy , told Upworthy. He explained that people pleasing is an adaptive personality trait . How people pleasing develops “It is simply a response learned due to direct and indirect messages that being helpful, likeable, or agreeable is safer and more beneficial to the social companionship and love that we all seek in relationships,” he added. People pleasing often develops in childhood as a defense mechanism for survival. “As a child, we may intuitively know that we need to help our parents get their needs met before they will meet our basic needs,” Shari B. Kaplan , LCSW, founder and clinical director of Cannectd Wellness, told Upworthy. “Or sometimes it just means meeting their needs or a sibling’s needs so you can be emotionally or physically safe in the house,” she continued. Hidden strengths of people pleasers While people pleasing may come with downsides, it also comes with many strengths. Here are five hidden strengths that people-pleasers likely possess: Hidden Strength #1: They are attuned to the needs and emotions of others “People pleasers are extremely invested in attending to others and making them feel good,” said Dr. Dillon. “They tend to develop a spidey-sense of sorts and are highly attuned to the needs of people around them and the feelings that they have,” he added. In turn, this gives people-pleasers a one-up on seeing others and attracting people to them. “This sensitivity and awareness of cues, energy, and body language make them more supportive, attentive, empathetic, and thoughtful than most,” Dr. Dillon explained. “We tend to gravitate towards them instinctively because of how they make us feel,” he continued. Hidden strength #2: They can see more than one perspective “Many people pleasers instinctively consider how a decision or an interaction might affect someone else,” Kaplan said. “That ability to look beyond their own immediate experiences can support collaboration, creative problem-solving, and common ground. Strength becomes more sustainable when they include their own needs in the picture,” she added. Hidden strength #3: They are collaborative “People pleasers are motivated not to let others down, and this usually presents as strong follow-through, thorough preparation, flexibility, and a low ego,” Jessica Gordon, LCSW, psychotherapist and owner of JNG Therapy , told Upworthy. “These qualities make for great teammates, colleagues, partners, and friends—the type of person others feel confident they can count on. This kind of dependability and consistency builds trust, which is the foundation of any strong relationship or team,” she continued. Hidden Strength #4: They are skilled at navigating relationships and conflict Dr. Dillon explained that people pleasers work to avoid conflict and navigate relationships seamlessly. “As such, they are attentive to connecting with us via common ground; they are often open-minded to differing perspectives and compromising,” he said. “They work to encourage collaboration and avoid disagreements in a way that makes us feel seen and heard. Since this is often experienced as pleasant, we lean into these relationships and want to connect and collaborate as much as possible,” Dr. Dillon added. Hidden Strength #5: They are dependable “People pleasers will never let you down. When they commit, they stick to it because they care about how their actions may impact you,” explained Dr. Dillon. “So we experience relationships with them as dependable, considerate, and valuable, and we feel like they are a part of the community or family that we are trying to create,” he concluded. The post Psychologists say being a people pleaser actually has 5 hidden strengths appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: What happened after the Big Bang? A team of physicists, harnessing the James Webb and Nancy Grace Roman space telescopes, are working to visualize the answer to that question using a novel computer simulation called Lumina. And they’re sharing some pretty stellar images and videos in the process. A new study out of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics introduces Lumina, which provides an unprecedented look at how the universe may have formed. The simulation harkens back to the nascent universe, from the dark ages that followed the Big Bang through the next 2 billion years of cosmic evolution. “The early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” lead author Oliver Zier said in a statement , crediting the James Webb scope. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.” Lumina collaboration A visualization of hydrogen re-ionization Those predictions focus on how the first galaxies, stars, and other cosmic structures were able to form amid a period of total darkness. Per a press release from MIT, the effect of the Big Bang was such that no light or radiation could pass through the “shroud” of neutral hydrogen created by the rapid expansion event. Eventually, however, two massive transformations occurred: the re-ionization of hydrogen and the re-ionization of helium. Hydrogen re-ionization refers to the era when the first stars were able to emit enough ultraviolet light to strip the neutral hydrogen of its electrons, preventing it from absorbing photons and thus “allowing light to travel freely.” Similarly, helium re-ionization refers to the breaking apart of neutral helium via high-energy light, something thought to have been fueled by supermassive black holes. The simulation captures these two essential processes in detail for the first time. Lumina collaboration A visualization of helium re-ionization “Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale re-ionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations,” study co-author Mark Vogelsberger said in the press release. He added the detail is unparalleled: “Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this. The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation.” Looking ahead, the team is making Lumina available to the scientific community to compare its simulations with real-world snapshots taken by new and future telescopes and tell a more complete story of how the first galaxies, stars, and structures of the universe may have formed. items.descriptionOriginal: In the never-ending quest to understand ourselves better , or at least have just one more distraction from whatever it is we should be doing, here comes the animal personality test . And the craziest part is (at least for me), it’s kind of accurate. The truth is, these days anyone can create their own personality tests. (And they do… and I’ve taken them.) Which Sex and the City character are you? Who is your inner Marvel superhero? What color is your heart? (Carrie, Ant Man, and black respectively.) Where this quiz actually came from But this particular animal archetype quiz, in actuality, is a model introduced in 1990 by Gary Smalley , a best-selling family-relationships author and counselor who died in 2016. Co-created by John Trent, who holds a PhD, the two wrote a book called The Two Sides of Love , which was revised in 2019 as The Two Sides of Love: The Secret to Valuing Differences . The idea is to strike a balance between the tender, “soft” side of love and the “hard,” more direct side. After taking the quiz provided in the book (and now online), one can find out if their temperament is the lion, the beaver, the otter, or the golden retriever . Even though it was written as a love-based tool, this personality test is often mentioned in the corporate world as a way to find out how people relate in the workforce. Jasper Rose, a financial recruiting agency, shared the quiz on their website , but notes, “This model should be taken with a pinch of salt. These animal categories describe the natural leaning of your temperament. In other words, they aren’t entirely fixed, as personalities are flexible and change over time and people are complex.” ( So something an otter would say.) Without further ado, the personality test can be taken (among many places) through this Michigan State University worksheet: Gary Smalley and John Trent’s personality test. Photo credit: Michigan State University A few things to know before you take it As with most personality tests, these questions can be tricky, since more than one answer will often apply. For example, one question asks that you rank what best describes you from the following: “likes authority, enthusiastic, sensitive feelings, likes instructions.” Another: “Takes charge, takes risks, loyal, accurate.” It’s possible to relate to all four statements equally, making this a flawed test. But if you’re in it for a lighthearted look at something that may vaguely describe you, here’s a breakdown of the results: The Lion These, according to the test, are the natural-born leaders. They are confident, take-charge, strong, and independent. From the Jasper Rose website: “ Strengths: visionary, persistent, practical, productive, initiates change and projects, communicates directly, enjoys being challenged, strong-willed, independent, decisive, leader. Weaknesses: Insensitive/cold, sarcastic, self-sufficient, impatient, stubborn, overlooks risks, controlling at times, can be too direct.” An educational worksheet on the Community Engaged Learning website (Michigan State University) adds that lions “are great at initiating communication, but not great at listening.” It adds that their natural desires are “freedom, authority, variety, difficult assignments, opportunity for advancement.” The Otter These are our happy social types. According to Jasper Rose, “They are often energetic and enthusiastic, with a tendency to be playful and enjoy humor. Otters are generally creative and enjoy trying new things but may struggle with follow-through. They value relationships and are often empathetic and compassionate towards others.” “ Strengths: Outgoing, optimistic, personable, communicator, dreamer, responsive, warm, friendly, talkative, enthusiastic, compassionate. Weaknesses: Undisciplined, unproductive, exaggerative, egocentric, unstable, struggle with follow-through, impulsive, needs social approval, easily offended.” The Center for Relationship Education adds, “Otters find it easy to be soft on people. It is also easy for them to be soft on problems. Otters need to learn to say ‘No’ and provide the hard-side balance of healthy boundary setting.” The Beaver These are our go-tos for decisive, detail-oriented people who actually enjoy structure and routine. Jasper Rose describes them this way: “Beavers tend to be cautious and risk-averse, preferring to follow established procedures rather than taking chances. They are also known for their analytical skills and ability to organize complex information. However, they may struggle with flexibility and creativity, and may sometimes be perceived as overly critical or perfectionistic.” “ Strengths: Analytical, thorough, decision-maker, deliberate, self-disciplined, industrious, organized, aesthetic, sacrificing. Weaknesses: Moody, self-centered, touchy, negative, unsociable, critical, revengeful.” The educational handout adds that in terms of relationships, “Beavers are good listeners, communicate details, and are usually diplomatic.” The Golden Retriever These are our loyal, dependable friends/lovers. Per Jasper Rose, “They also tend to avoid conflict and prioritize maintaining harmony in their relationships. However, they may struggle with making decisions and taking action, and may sometimes come across as passive or indifferent.” “ Strengths: Calm, supportive, agreeable, easy-going, loyal, dependable, quiet, objective, diplomatic, humorous, values relationships, stable and consistent. Weaknesses: Selfish, stingy, indirect with others, resists change, procrastinator, unmotivated, lacks initiative, indecisive, fearful, worrier, can be co-dependent.” The Center for Relationship Education notes, “Goldens’ strong tendency toward the soft-side of love can lead to issues of co-dependence and enabling. Goldens need to learn to balance their natural soft-side with some hard-side qualities.” So which animal are you, really? As with most quizzes like these, most of us are a combination of traits not easily put into labeled boxes. If nothing else, it’s a creative way to get people thinking about how they interact with one another in a variety of situations. (Which is totally something a golden retriever like me would say.) This article originally appeared last year . It has been updated. The post A fun personality test determines ‘how you love’ based on your animal archetype appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Parents are people, too. Whether they subscribe to “ gentle parenting ” ideas or a more old-school approach , the truth is that they’re just doing their best. Sometimes they get it right, sometimes they make mistakes, and quite often, it’s hard for anyone to tell whether they’re doing a good job until years later. In September 2015, Heidi Johnson’s son, Aaron, was 13, deeply in adolescence, and in that stage where he’d frequently lash out and defy her at every turn. In one such instance, he stubbornly told her he shouldn’t have to deal with her rules and should be independent. So she wrote a strict but loving “Mom’s not a fool” letter. In the letter, she wrote that because he bragged about making money from his YouTube channel, he could buy back all of the things that she had purchased for him in the past and that he would also have to pay rent. Here is what was in the letter “Dear Aaron, Since you seem to have forgotten you are only 13, and I’m the parent, and that you won’t be controlled, I guess you will need a lesson in independence. Also, as you threw in my face that you are making money now, it will be easier to buy back all the items I bought for you in the past. If you would like your lamp/lightbulbs or access to the internet, you will need to pay your own share of costs. Rent – $430 Electricity – $116 Internet – $21 Food – $150″ The itemized bill totaled $717. She also added some additional chores that, if not accomplished, she would fine him $30. “He came home, saw the note, crumpled it on the floor, and stormed out of the apartment. I have always encouraged him to take a walk when he is upset so that he can collect his thoughts, so when we try to talk, we are able to talk, and not just yell at each other. I do the same thing — sometimes, I just need to walk away and collect myself. I am not above admitting that. He was still livid when he got home. He decided to stage a ‘sit in’in my room, where he did laugh at me and repeat, ‘Really? What are you going to do? You can’t take my stuff,’ etc. He was asked to leave my room, and when he could be respectful, and I was more calm, we would discuss it further. He went to his room, and after about an hour, he had removed some electronics and items I missed that he felt he should have to earn back for his behavior. He apologized and asked what could he do to make things better and start earning items back. He earned his comforter and some clothes right back. I did leave him some clothes to begin with, just not the ones he would want to wear every day. He also had some pillows and sheets, just not his favorite ones.” Then the internet got involved Johnson decided to post the letter in its entirety on Facebook, the way one does to friends for a laugh and connection. After all, the strategy had been a success! However, she neglected to make it “private,” and soon, comments and shares proliferated (more than 165,000 shares, according to KING 5 ), including admonishments from strangers who thought she was a bad parent. Now she had to deal with a bigger teenager: the internet and its commentariat. But Johnson remained level-headed and wrote another Facebook post, clarifying. “It’s out there; and I am not ashamed of what I wrote… I am not going to put my 13-year-oldon the street if he can’t pay his half of the rent. I am not wanting him to pay anything. I want him to take pride in his home, his space, and appreciate the gifts and blessings we have.” She explains that he is more grateful because of it, and also that he has slowly earned back things and dealt with sacrificing others. Then she lists her very organized and succinct rules of the house: 1. Do your best in school! I don’t expect a perfect 100%, but I do expect that you do your best and ask for help when you don’t understand something. 2. Homework and jobs need to be done before you can have screen time. 3. Jobs are emptying the trash, unloading the dishwasher, throwing away trash you make in the kitchen, rinsing dirty dishes, making your bed daily, pick up bedroom nightly, and cleaning your bathroom once a week. 4. You must complete two chores a day. Each day of the week with the exception of Sunday has a room that we work on cleaning. He has to pick two chores for that room. For example, if it is the living room he can choose two of the following options: dust, vacuum, polish furniture, clean windows, mop the floor. 5. Be respectful and kind with your words: no back talking, no cussing at me. 6. Keep good hygiene. 7. Make eye contact when being spoken to, and be an active listener. 8. Use proper manners. It seems that after a long conversation about what being independent truly means, the mother and son came to a deeper understanding and patched things up. “You know what.. this hasn’t hurt our relationship. He and I still talk as openly as ever. He has apologized multiple times… And… he is trying harder,” Johnson said. What experts say about tough love Tough love is a controversial topic in parenting circles. Some say it makes kids anxious and unsafe while others insist that it’s the only way to truly instill an understanding of consequences in young people. Experts say the best “tough love” enforces boundaries and consequences in order to teach tough life lessons, but is done with love and understanding rather than yelling, and it’s certainly never violent. That’s why it’s so powerful how Johnson took the time to cool herself down and write a firm but level-headed letter. It’s also important to remember that teens who rebel aren’t bad or ungrateful. The rebellion is a part of how they begin to establish their much-needed independence. She had plenty of supporters After the initial negative reaction to her post, Johnson’s story continued to spread and drew praise from other exasperated parents of teens: “Tough love is real love, he has a chance because of you,” one commenter wrote. “Good for you! He needs to appreciate everything you do! You are doing him a favor teaching him what it is to take care of himself and learn some respect,” wrote another. “Best parent I have read about in a very long time. Kids do not rule the house, adults rule the house. Thank you very much for being a great mom,” another said. At the time, Johnson’s son was earning things back little by little, and “appreciating it more than he did before,” she wrote. Aaron, who was 13 when the letter went viral in 2015, is now an adult. “This came down to a 13-year-old telling his mother she had no right to enforce certain rules, and had no place to ‘control’ him. I made the point to show what life would look like if I was not his ‘parent,’ but rather a ‘roommate.’ It was a lesson about gratitude and respect from the very beginning. Sometimes, you have to lose it all to realize how well you really had it.” This article originally appeared 11 years ago. It has been updated. The post Mom writes tough letter to rebellious, ‘independent’ 13-year-old son and gets unexpected response appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Bengaluru has a strange paradox: a city that floods every monsoon still struggles with water shortages. Watching its lakes disappear beneath concrete and waste, Harsha Tej decided to do something about it. He quit his job, picked up a shovel and began restoring the water bodies that once gave the city life. Through the BlueDot Foundation, Harsha has helped restore 18 lakes across Karnataka and plant more than 1.5 lakh native trees. From clearing invasive growth to rebuilding habitats, his work goes beyond beautifying lakes. Healthy lakes can support wildlife, help recharge groundwater and improve the landscape’s ability to manage rainwater. For Harsha, every restored lake brings Bengaluru a step closer to the city he remembers, where nature and urban life coexist. His journey shows how one person’s determination can inspire meaningful environmental change, one lake at a time. items.title: Από ένα πρόβλημα ταξινόμησης του 1972 στο DIGIPIN: Η ιστορία πίσω από τους 6-ψήφιους κωδικούς PIN της Ινδίας
items.titleOriginal: From a 1972 Sorting Problem to DIGIPIN: The Story Behind India’s 6-digit PIN Codes
items.description: Μια επιστολή για επιστήμονες στον ερευνητικό σταθμό Maitri της Ινδίας στην Ανταρκτική φέρει τον ίδιο κωδικό PIN με το Panaji , 403001, επειδή το πολικό ταχυδρομείο ταξιδεύει μέσω του Εθνικού Κέντρου Πολικής και Ωκεανικής Έρευνας στο Vasco στη Γκόα. Η ιδιορρυθμία δείχνει πόση δουλειά κάνουν οι έξι αριθμοί για τα ταχυδρομεία 1,64 lakh που λειτουργεί σήμερα η India Post και την ιστορία αυτού…
items.descriptionOriginal: A letter for scientists at India's Maitri research station in Antarctica carrie the same PIN code as Panaji , 403001, because polar mail travels through the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research at Vasco in Goa. The quirk shows how much work six numerals do for the 1.64 lakh post offices that India Post operates today, and the story of that code begins with a sorting problem more than 50 years old. A country of similar place names At Independence in 1947, India had 23,344 post offices, mostly in cities, but the network had to keep pace with a growing country. The Postal Index Number, introduced on 15 August, 1972, aimed to ease the sorting and delivery of mail in a land where different places often share the same or similar names and letters arrive in a wide variety of languages. The idea came from Shriram Bhikaji Velankar, an additional secretary in the Ministry of Communications and a senior member of the Posts and Telegraphs Board. Velankar also wrote Sanskrit poetry, received the President's Award for Sanskrit in 1996, chaired the Indipex stamp exhibition in New Delhi in 1973, and retired from government service on 31 December, 1973. What each of the six digits tells you The length follows from the hierarchy of the code, which gives one digit to the zone, one to the sub-region, one to the sorting district, and three to the delivery post office. The first digit names one of eight regional zones, running from 1 for Delhi, Haryana, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to 8 for Bihar and Jharkhand, while 9 belongs to the Army Postal Service. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times /AI-Generated collage) The second digit narrows the zone to a sub-region, and the third, read together with the first two, marks a sorting district headquartered at the main post office of the largest city in the area. Goa's 403 carves out a small piece of the 40 to 44 band that otherwise belongs to Maharashtra. The final three digits identify the delivery office, and a busy office that splits in two receives the next available code. Each PIN maps to exactly one delivery post office, which receives the mail for every sub-office and branch office in its jurisdiction. A single PIN code can therefore cover a cluster of villages, and two neighbouring delivery offices share only their first four digits. The same code at the edges of the map The structure holds even at altitude, where the post office in Hikkim, a Spiti Valley village , stands at 4,400 metres and closes for six months each winter when snow cuts off the settlement. Its code, 172114, places it in Himachal Pradesh through the prefix 17, and the office ranks among the highest in the world. The floating post office on Dal Lake began as a postal boat in 1953. It belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. Photograph: ( Lifeandtrendz ) The system also reaches Dal Lake in Srinagar, where the floating post office , which began as a postal boat serving lake communities in 1953, belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. The ninth zone serves a different kind of address, because the Army Postal Service runs field post offices serving the Army, Navy and Air Force across the country. The 2017 Salute a Soldier campaign, organised by India Post and the Postcrossing Society of India in Bengaluru, directed postcards of thanks to around 1,000 Army units. Why six digits still matter The model has a precedent abroad, because the United States introduced its Zone Improvement Plan code on 1 July, 1963, when letters passed through about 17 sorting stops. India followed nine years later with a hierarchy of its own, and its relevance remains clear whenever someone orders food or a parcel online. India Post has since added DIGIPIN, a 10-character code developed with IIT Hyderabad and ISRO that identifies a 4 m by 4 m square, and it complements the six-digit code rather than replacing it. The PIN still tells a sorter which zone, district and office should handle a letter, while DIGIPIN tells a delivery person which doorstep to find. Anyone can check a code using the lookup on India Post's website, and no PIN begins with 0, because the nine zones run from 1 to 9. Taken together, the digits turn an address into a route. A PIN such as 403001 tells a sorter that the mail belongs to the western zone, Goa's sorting district and the Panaji head office, and it does so without a word of any local language. That efficiency, which began on 15 August, 1972, still reaches from the largest cities to the highest hamlets. Sources ' Government expands postal network with 10,170 post offices over last 11 years ': by All India Radio News, Published on 10 December, 2025 ' What is DIGIPIN, India's new high-tech address system from Dept of Posts? ': By The Week, Published on 31 May, 2025

items.descriptionOriginal: People are drowning in eco-friendly swag—cloth tote bags, reusable water bottles, recycled notebooks, sustainable hotel toiletries, and on and on—distributed by organizations and companies eager to demonstrate their environmental bona fides. What might be even more sustainable than manufacturing and distributing all these eco-friendly products is to just…stop. The trouble is that consumers have trouble giving brands credit for such restraint, a quirk of human psychology that researchers dub “sustainable additive bias” in a new paper. “Companies that genuinely try to take eco-friendly actions, such as reducing packaging or promotional giveaways, are often not rewarded,” says study team member Linda Lemarié , associate professor of marketing at Audencia Business School in France. “What we don’t see is hard to take into consideration, and reduction leaves nothing visible, even though it’s often the best strategy from an environmental standpoint.” In the paper, Lemarié and her colleagues conducted nine different studies to demonstrate how this bias works—and what companies can do about it. The studies included a field experiment in which hotel guests rated the sustainability of the room they had stayed in, a lab experiment in which business school students chose gifts to hand out to trade show attendees, and seven online investigations in which a total of more than 2,900 participants were asked to evaluate complimentary hotel toiletries, hair care sets, music festival welcome bags, and other collections of products. Overall, the studies show that consumers see businesses as more sustainable when they provide more eco-friendly items rather than when they remove unnecessary ones—even though subtracting can lead to true: Information that confirms your beliefs...or information repeated over and over? “We were first surprised by the robustness and consistency of the effect across different contexts and with different metrics,” Lemarié says. For example, study participants judged a hotel room stocked with a large selection of eco-friendly toiletries as more sustainable than a room with a more modest set of eco-friendly products. They also judged a limited-edition tea box to which eco-friendly tea filters had been added as more sustainable than one from which they had been removed. “Then we were also surprised by the bias’s resistance to knowledge,” Lemarié says. When items weren’t labeled as being environmentally friendly , participants identified bundles with more items as being less sustainable than those with fewer. “This means that people do indeed correctly associate ‘addition with ‘less environmentally friendly.’” But when the question of sustainability comes into play, people seem to use visible components as indicators of companies’ effort. The more items, the more effort, and the more effort, the more sustainability—at least, according to our imperfect brains. Several of the experiments suggest sustainable additive bias can be counteracted when companies prioritize highly recognizable items as sustainability signals (that is, a refillable water bottle counts more than biodegradable glitter). One hints that explaining when items have been removed for environmental reasons might help, too. But accomplishing this in the real world could be tricky, Lemarié says. “The question our research leaves open is how to effectively demonstrate, without appearing hypocritical or making people skeptical, that reducing elements of a product offering, and thus offering less, is a genuine effort in favor of the environment.” Source: Lemarié L. et al. “ The more, the better? items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with Vibha. For a student pursuing a diploma, an internship can be the bridge between what they learn in a classroom and what they will eventually do at work. But finding the right opportunity is not always straightforward. Nikhil Kumar, a 21-year-old B.Tech CSE student from Punjab, had come across internships that required candidates to hold a bachelor's degree or pay fees to gain experience. After completing his diploma in 2025, he chose to pursue a bachelor's degree. The experience made him think about the barriers other diploma students might face. At Government Polytechnic College, Talwara, Nikhil was already putting his coding skills to use. Alongside his faculty mentor, Sukeeratpal Singh, he was developing a college management system to simplify administrative work. When Vibha's Programme Management Unit (PMU) learnt about the project, it saw an opportunity to build on it. The team was working on a semester-long internship programme in which students would spend their final semester working in industry rather than attending regular theory classes. Together, they adapted the system to help colleges monitor students' progress throughout this practical training. Sukeeratpal Singh and the Vibha PMU team helped Nikhil develop Place Intern to track students' internship progress. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The project became Place Intern, a portal that brings student internship records, faculty visits and progress reports together. "I was also curious whether whatever I was building would be used in the real world," Nikhil says. The project gave him the chance to find out. With guidance from his faculty mentor, Sukeeratpal Singh, and support from Vibha's (PMU), which works with Punjab's technical education department, Nikhil helped develop his college's internship management system into a tool that could be used by other institutions. How a college project found a purpose beyond campus At Government Polytechnic College, Talwara, Singh had been encouraging students to explore technology beyond their regular coursework. In 2023, he started a student club where interested students could spend additional time learning, experimenting, and helping one another. Nikhil stood out for his willingness to take on work independently. "He was always the one who finished the work first," Singh recalls. The two began working on a college management system that could make certain administrative processes easier to handle. They planned its features, decided how it would work and tested it over several weeks. The project caught the attention of Vibha's PMU when team member Abhay Vashisht visited the college. The team was working on the policy and programme design for a semester-long internship initiative for students in technical education. As they considered how the programme would work on the ground, they began identifying possible implementation challenges, including how colleges could monitor students throughout their internships. Nikhil's understanding of the college environment, combined with the PMU's inputs on the internship programme, helped shape the portal into a tool that could support its implementation. Nikhil built the parts that store and manage information, tested the portal, put it online and kept it running. Singh helped him understand the college workflows the system needed to support, while the PMU team shared the programme requirements, developed an initial outline for the portal and worked closely with him to refine its design through testing and feedback. Place Intern brings student progress reports, faculty visits and internship records onto one platform, reducing dependence on separate spreadsheets and paper-based submissions. Building the portal also meant learning how to work with the people who would use it. Nikhil showed faculty members how to use it, wrote instructions and made changes based on their feedback. He had to think about how different people would use the system and what information they needed to access. Place Intern currently helps colleges track students undertaking internships during their final semester, when they work in industry in place of regular theory classes. It does not serve as a placement portal that matches students with employers or guarantees them internships. Its four types of users each see the information they need. Faculty members can record monthly visits to students at their internship workplaces, while students submit reports on their progress. The principal closely monitors the tasks faculty and students undertake, while the Directorate in Chandigarh uses dashboard access to track progress and review updates. "By bringing these records together, the portal reduces dependence on separate spreadsheets and paper-based submissions," adds Nikhil. Building the portal taught Nikhil how to create something people could actually use, and how working closely with those using it could help make it better. 'Students need to apply their classroom knowledge' For students like Nikhil, finding an internship is one part of a larger challenge: turning a technical qualification into the skills and confidence needed to enter the workforce. Mridul Dhyani, who works with Vibha's PMU in Punjab, says diploma programmes have faced challenges around industry acceptance, student retention and employability. "Students may understand technical concepts in the classroom, but they also need opportunities to apply that knowledge and become familiar with workplace expectations," he shares. For students in rural areas, finding these opportunities can be especially difficult. Colleges may have fewer employers nearby, and students may not have family or professional networks that can connect them to industries. Sukeeratpal has seen these challenges through his work in teaching and placements. Earlier, students often had to approach companies and establish industry connections themselves. Colleges also lacked a consistent way to track internships and follow students' progress. Faculty members can use Place Intern to record monthly visits to students at their internship workplaces and track their progress during practical training. "Earlier it was in the minds of the children that a diploma is enough," Sukeeratpal says. "Now our priority has become to make the students job-ready." Addressing these gaps means helping students find openings while also introducing structured internships, strengthening industry engagement, updating curricula and developing the communication and practical skills they need at work. Place Intern helps colleges keep track of students during their internships. Finding an internship is the first step, but colleges also need to know how students are progressing, whether their training is going as planned and if they are gaining useful experience. The portal is part of a larger effort to help students build the skills they need for employment. Taking a student-built portal beyond the classroom The wider effort is supported by Vibha, which works towards ensuring high-quality public education for every child. Its mission is to improve learning levels in government schools by identifying, supporting and scaling proven solutions. It works with governments, implementation partners, educators and communities to strengthen different parts of the education system, including early reading and maths, teacher training, classroom materials, technology, record-keeping and tracking progress. In Punjab, the work focuses on technical education. "The underlying approach is similar: understand where the system is falling short, work with government teams and institutions to address those gaps, and support solutions that can become part of regular practice," adds Mridul. The Programme Management Unit (PMU) helps put this approach into practice. Working alongside government departments and educational institutions, it listens to people at colleges, identifies what needs attention, helps develop solutions and sees them put to use. For Place Intern, the PMU saw how the college's existing technology project could help manage semester-long internships. The team worked with Nikhil and Singh to understand what colleges needed, adapt the portal accordingly, and test and improve it for everyday use. Through its PMU, Vibha works with Punjab's technical education department and polytechnic colleges to bridge the gap between education and employment. The aim is to make sure the tool works for the people who will depend on it. Faculty members, college leaders and department officials need to understand how it fits into their responsibilities, while students need a clear process for submitting reports and being monitored during their internships. "We just don't work towards plans," Dhyani says. "Our work starts with a plan, but it doesn't stop till we complete the loop." That follow-through matters when a solution is expected to last beyond its development. Training, feedback and institutional ownership can determine whether a new system becomes part of everyday practice or remains a one-off project. How a 2-week maths course became part of a bigger effort Alongside efforts to help students find internships, the wider initiative has also focused on making classroom learning more relevant to their needs. Across 91 government polytechnic colleges in Punjab, the wider initiative has reached 5,921 students in FY 2026, with semester internships introduced in six courses. These numbers reflect the initiative's combined work across several interventions, not Place Intern alone. Some of the changes began with a simple question: what were students struggling with in the classroom? When mathematics emerged as a challenge, the team introduced a two-week bridge course to help students strengthen their basics. According to Dhyani, the results showed up the following year, when the proportion of students passing the subject rose from 16% to 31%. A two-week mathematics bridge course helped address gaps in students' foundational learning, with the reported pass rate rising from 16% to 31%. English classes saw a change, too. Instead of placing most of the emphasis on literature and grammar, the revised curriculum focused more on functional English and everyday conversations. The reported pass rate rose from 45% to 92%. Dhyani recalls that some teachers were initially hesitant about the shift, but later noticed that students were participating more actively in class. The programme also includes faculty training, entrepreneurship education and efforts to build stronger industry links. Each intervention addresses a different gap, but the approach remains the same: understand the problem, involve the people affected and find a solution that works within the existing system. Singh has also seen how easily industry relationships can fall apart when they depend on a single staff member who later moves on. By keeping in touch with employers and sharing responsibility across staff, colleges can make these partnerships last and give students more reliable workplace opportunities. The next step: bringing colleges and employers together Place Intern has begun supporting the tracking of semester internships at the college level. Profiles for the first batch of more than 1,500 students have been uploaded, with profiles for a further batch of over 1,700 also being prepared. These figures indicate students being recorded for tracking, not that all have secured internships through the portal. The longer-term ambition is to make it easier for colleges and employers to connect. A planned statewide platform is intended to help industries share their requirements and allow institutions to identify relevant opportunities for students across polytechnics, industrial training institutes and degree colleges. For Nikhil, developing Place Intern has offered a different kind of practical learning. He has had to understand how people use technology, respond to feedback and keep a system functioning beyond its initial development. Beyond internship tracking, the wider initiative is working to improve functional English, strengthen industry connections and help students develop practical skills for the workplace. Singh sees the project as a reason to give students more room to experiment, with faculty members providing the guidance needed to turn an idea into something useful. The next test is whether these systems can become part of everyday institutional practice, making it easier to monitor internships and build stronger links between education and employment. Nikhil's experience began with developing a college management system, but working with the PMU gave the project a wider purpose. For Nikhil, the experience has meant building his own skills while working on a tool that could make the path from education to employment easier for students who follow. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Blue-Green Corridor Transforms a Flood-Prone Waterway in Thimphu in Bhutan Reading Time: 3 minutes Bhutan’s capital is transforming the flood-prone Memorial Chorten stream into a blue-green corridor that combines flood protection, ecological restoration, and inclusive public space. A new blue-green corridor is taking shape along Thimphu’s Memorial Chorten stream in Bhutan. City planners want to turn the flood-prone waterway into a safer, greener public space. The stream flows past some of the capital’s most visited landmarks. The Memorial Chorten stream is one of five key waterways identified in Thimphu’s long-term city plan . It connects the city center to the Wang Chhu River. Rapid construction and heavier rains have made the corridor increasingly prone to flooding. The stream passes near the National Memorial Chorten, a well-known Buddhist stupa in the capital. It also runs by the Royal Bhutan Police Headquarters and the Changlimithang area. Despite this central location, much of the corridor remains hard to access today. Queen Ashi Phuntsho Choden Wangchuck built the Memorial Chorten decades ago in memory of the third king. Today it stands as one of Bhutan’s most visited religious sites. Its surrounding stream corridor sees heavy foot traffic from residents and visitors alike. Flooding has become a growing concern across Thimphu in recent years. A flash flood tore through the nearby Dechencholing community in 2025. Officials say the city, originally planned for a much smaller population, now faces mounting climate pressure. Thimphu Thromde, the city’s municipal government, has now finalized a revitalization design plan for the site. The project blends engineered flood controls with nature-based solutions to build a blue-green corridor. Together, these measures aim to lower flood risk while restoring the stream’s ecological health. Planned work includes restoring riparian plants and naturalizing the stream channel itself. New retention ponds would capture stormwater before it floods nearby streets. Waste interception systems would also help keep pollution out of the waterway. New walking trails, viewing areas, and solar-powered lighting would open the future blue-green corridor to the public. Better pedestrian paths are also expected to improve safety around the stream. Recreational spaces are planned to encourage residents to spend time outdoors. Thimphu’s planned blue-green corridor will combine naturalized stream channels, stormwater retention ponds, and waste interception systems with solar-powered walking trails, viewing areas, and recreational spaces, turning a flood-prone urban waterway into a safe, accessible public amenity. Photo by Dechen Wangmo, courtesy of UNDP . Inclusive design guided much of the planning process from the start. Planners want the corridor to feel safe and accessible for women, children, and older residents. The site’s design also considered people with disabilities. The design plan came together through the Disaster Resilient Infrastructure Project. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) supported the effort. Funding came through the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, or CDRI, and its Infrastructure Resilience Accelerator Fund. A separate ongoing initiative will help carry the design into construction. That project, backed by UNDP and the Global Environment Facility, focuses on wider urban climate resilience. Reports indicate Bhutan has allocated roughly $24 million toward related stream corridor work. That broader initiative also covers more than 30 kilometers of stormwater drains across central Thimphu. The Global Environment Facility and the Royal Government of Bhutan jointly fund the six-year effort. Together, these projects mark one of the largest urban resilience pushes in the country’s history. Engineers, landscape architects, and gender specialists all contributed to the design. Local agencies held site assessments and community consultations before finalizing plans. That collaborative process shaped decisions on everything from drainage to lighting. Officials describe the effort as one of Bhutan’s first projects to combine several goals at once. Disaster resilience, ecological restoration, and inclusive public space design all come together in a single corridor. Few urban projects in the region have attempted such an integrated approach. The project supports goals set out in Bhutan’s National Adaptation Plan. It also echoes the country’s long-term strategy for low-emission, climate-resilient development . Urban human settlements remain a key focus area under both documents. Officials hope the corridor can serve as a practical model for other Bhutanese cities facing similar flood risks and growing pressure on urban waterways. Lessons from Thimphu could soon help guide blue-green corridor projects along other rivers and streams, showing how restoring natural waterways can strengthen urban resilience while creating healthier public spaces. For a small mountain kingdom, restoring one stream could provide valuable lessons and help protect many more communities from future flooding. The post Blue-Green Corridor Transforms a Flood-Prone Waterway in Thimphu in Bhutan appeared first on Happy Eco News .
