items.descriptionOriginal: Apapang, Alang and Ahu may weigh just 150 grams each, but they have some serious frequent-flyer miles to clock. They are Amur Falcons. In November 2025, these three Amur falcons were fitted with satellite tags by scientists from the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) in Tamenglong district, Manipur, to track their epic journey from Northeast India to Africa. Every November, thousands of these tiny birds of prey take off from roosting sites in Manipur and Nagaland , cross the Indian mainland and head over the Arabian Sea. Their itinerary? Thousands of kilometres, days over open water and no airport lounges in sight. Since the Amurs have created a mini-sensation with their incredible journey, I did a short Q&A with Dr Suresh from @wii_india who leads this remarkable tracking project. Here are a few fascinating insights Q. Why do Amur Falcons migrate? A. Migration is a natural survival strategy. Many species, including the Amur Falcon, move seasonally to escape harsh weather, seek richer feeding grounds, or find suitable breeding habitats. Over evolutionary time, individuals that migrated had higher survival and reproductive success which is why migration persists in certain species even today. Q. Why is tracking their migration important? A. Tracking with lightweight electronic tags helps scientists understand the exact routes and flight paths these birds follow, the environmental factors influencing their journey, and the critical stopover sites they depend on. It also helps identify threats along the way from habitat loss to hunting and provides vital insights into how Climate Change is shifting migration patterns worldwide. Q. How do Amur Falcons survive such long flights without food or water? A. Before they begin their transcontinental journey, Amur Falcons stop over at select sites in Northeast India, especially Nagaland and Manipur. Their arrival coincides with the mass emergence of termites a rich, high-protein food source. Here, they undergo hyperphagia or intense pre-migratory fattening, building reserves that sustain them through their nonstop oceanic flights where no food or water is available. Q. Do they take breaks while crossing the sea? A. No. Amur Falcons are terrestrial birds and cannot land on water. Once they leave the Indian coast, they undertake an uninterrupted flight across the Arabian Sea, a remarkable non-stop journey covering nearly 3000 km. — Supriya Sahu IAS (@supriyasahuias) November 17, 2025 Their journey revealed how a bird barely heavier than a smartphone can cross thousands of kilometres of open sea. It also highlighted why Northeast India is an important stopover along their migratory route. A journey tracked across continents On 11 November 2025, WII scientists fitted Apapang, an adult male, Alang, a young female, and Ahu, an adult female, with lightweight satellite transmitters weighing approximately 3.5–4 grams. The birds took flight the following day. The tracking updates were shared by Supriya Sahu, Tamil Nadu's Additional Chief Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forests, on social media. Apapang covered approximately 6,100 kilometres in six days and eight hours. Alang travelled around 5,600 kilometres in six days and 14 hours, while Ahu covered approximately 5,100 kilometres in five days before reaching the Horn of Africa. Their routes differed, but all three completed remarkable journeys across the Indian mainland and the Arabian Sea. Subsequent tracking updates placed Apapang in Tanzania, Alang in Kenya and Ahu in northern Somalia. The birds' journeys provided researchers with valuable information about their movements , flight durations and stopover behaviour. Why do they stop in Northeast India? The answer lies in an insect that emerges in enormous numbers after the monsoon: termites. Amur falcons breed in parts of eastern Russia, northeastern China and Mongolia before migrating south towards their wintering grounds in Africa. During their autumn journey , Northeast India provides an important opportunity to feed and build up the energy reserves needed for their demanding flight. A 2024 study published in the Journal of Raptor Research, titled Prey Species in the Diet of the Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis) During Autumn Passage Stopover in Northeast India , investigated what the birds eat at their stopover sites. The birds' journeys provided researchers with valuable information about their movements, flight durations and stopover behaviour. Photograph: (Bhupender Yadav-Wildlife Institute of India) Led by researchers including Suresh Kumar of WII, the team examined approximately 1,200 regurgitated pellets collected at Pangti, Yaongyimchen and Hakhizhe in Nagaland during October and November 2017 and 2018. These pellets contained indigestible remains of the birds' prey. By examining them, researchers found that two species of subterranean termites, Odontotermes feae and Odontotermes horni , formed a substantial part of their diet. The findings help explain why the birds congregate in the region. Termites provide protein and energy that the falcons convert into fat reserves before embarking on their long oceanic flight. Researchers estimated that a million falcons could consume two billion termites in just over a fortnight. A stopover that matters beyond autumn The importance of Northeast India extends beyond the autumn migration. In a second study, published in the Journal of Threatened Taxa on 26 March 2024, researchers Tapak Tamir, Abprez Thungwon Kimsing and Daniel Mize documented repeated summer sightings of Amur falcons in D'Ering Memorial Wildlife Sanctuary in Arunachal Pradesh. Here is the New Year Amur Falcon Migration -Very long Q&A Part II Q1. What is the longest non-stop distance covered by these satellite-tagged Amur Falcons? A: Published tracking shows Amur Falcons can do multi-day, non-stop flights of approx. 5,600–6,000 km during the India Africa leg, depending on the individual & year. Also, peer-reviewed/technical tracking confirms their open-sea crossings can be about 2,364–3,138 km (Somalia India), typically completed in roughly 44–80 hours. Q2. Do satellite tags interfere with their flight, health, or mating? A: Properly fitted tags are designed to minimise interference, but no tag is "zero-impact.". Best practice is to keep transmitter mass very small relative to body weight and use well-tested harness designs; the recent India work has been described as using very lightweight transmitters (a few grams). However, ethical review, careful fitting, and post-deployment evaluation should be done & is being done Q3. Do jet streams or high-altitude winds help them on this journey? A: Yes winds are a major part of the "physics" that makes the journey possible. The best-documented help is from seasonal monsoon tailwinds and strong, persistent wind systems over the Arabian Sea/Indian Ocean that can provide sustained push. Q4. How many other falcons are "accompanying" these famous three? A: These famous three are just the tagged individuals we can follow in reality, Amur Falcons migrate and roost in huge aggregations, often tens of thousands to over 100,000 at key stopovers, and broader estimates discuss movements involving very large numbers of birds across the flyway. Q5. Why have these three gone to different destinations? A: It's common for individuals of the same species to winter in different areas within southern/eastern Africa. Differences can be driven by wind and weather, refuelling success and timing at stopovers, individual strategy/experience (age, condition, learned routes) etc. Q6. When will they return and what route will they take? A: In broad terms, Amur Falcons winter in Africa and then move north in late winter/early spring, reaching breeding regions in northeast Asia around May–June. Routes can differ between autumn vs spring, and tracking shows spring and autumn ocean crossings can follow different lines. Q7. Does part of the falcon's brain "sleep" during the long flight? A: We have strong evidence that some birds can sleep in flight (including unihemispheric sleep) famously shown in frigatebirds. For Amur Falcons specifically, it's not proven. Q8. How do they decide their destination, and do they return to the same places each year? A: The best-supported explanation is a mix of: Innate navigation programmes (genetically guided ) Environmental cues (winds, weather, geography, magnetic and celestial cues), learning/experience (older birds often show more consistent routes). Satellite work indicates the species follows remarkably consistent large-scale timing and corridors, even though individuals may vary. Q9. What do they eat to fuel such massive journeys? A: During the crucial Northeast India stopover, studies show they are highly insectivorous, with termites often dominant, along with other insect groups exactly the kind of high-abundance prey that allows rapid fattening before an ocean crossing. This is why protecting stopover habitats (and the insect "boom" they depend on) is so important. Q10. Is Ahu expected to move further? Why she is stationery ? A. Periods of little movement usually indicate resting or feeding in suitable habitat. This is normal behaviour and not a cause for concern Q11. How long does the GPS tag stay on the bird? A. The tag is fixed as a backpack & expected to stay for long, however this may come off from prolonged wear and tear, the tags may also stop transmitting after prolonged battery use. As told to @supriyasahuias by @sureshwii @wii_india #AmurFalconMigration video - The stopover tagging site in Manipur — Supriya Sahu IAS (@supriyasahuias) January 4, 2026 The sanctuary, in East Siang district, covers approximately 190 square kilometres and consists largely of grasslands, alongside riverine and subtropical forests. The researchers documented sightings, including one in May, that suggested the sanctuary could serve as a refuelling site during the birds' return towards their breeding grounds. From hunted birds to protected visitors The falcons' journey has also become a story of community-led conservation. In 2012, large-scale hunting of Amur falcons around Pangti village in Nagaland drew national and international attention. In response, the Wildlife Institute of India, forest departments and local communities worked to understand the birds' migration and protect their stopover sites. Tracking efforts began in 2013. Over time, communities in parts of Nagaland and Manipur became important partners in protecting the birds. The falcons, once hunted in large numbers, increasingly became a source of local pride. Their migration demonstrates how wildlife conservation depends on connected habitats and people working across regions. A bird may breed in Asia, refuel in Northeast India and spend the winter in Africa, but its survival depends on the safety of each place along the way. For the Amur falcon, the seasonal emergence of termites is more than a feeding opportunity. It is a chance to prepare for a flight across continents. Protecting the landscapes where that preparation happens is essential to ensuring the journey continues. Sources: '6,000 km in six days: How WII tracked a trio of Amur falcons across continents' : By Malavika Jayadeep,Published on 26 November 2025 'Prey Species in the Diet of the Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis) during Autumn Passage Stopover in Northeast India' : By Amarjeet Kaur, Alex Jacob, Deven Mehta, R. Suresh Kumar, Published on 13 June 2024 'D'Ering Memorial Wildlife Sanctuary, a significant flyway and a preferred stopover (refuelling) site during the return migration of the Amur Falcon Falco amurensis' : By Tapak Tamir, Abprez Thungwon Kimsing, Daniel Mize, Published on 26 March 2024

items.descriptionOriginal: P atty Spillman and her husband farm over 400 acres of corn, soybeans and wheat in central Ohio. Both have lived in the area all their lives; his family has been on the land since 1861. In 2023, a developer proposed a data center on a nearby farm. “[The community] fought them off,” she says. “But I always kind of knew that just because the one data center had left, that didn’t mean it was going to be gone forever. Someone else was going to be right on their heels.” She was right. Less than two years later, another developer started moving forward with plans for a much larger data center, located across the street from her farm. Headwaters, a Texas-based company, wanted to annex land in Pleasant Township (where Spillman lives) and nearby Jackson Township for a 300-plus acre facility in Grove City. This is a story playing out in communities across the U.S., where A.I. demands have rapidly accelerated the need for data centers, along with the extraordinary amounts of water and energy that they consume. But residents are pushing back, advocating for more community input, insisting that the data facilities cover the full cost of locating there (such as local grid infrastructure upgrades), and even calling for outright moratoriums. Patty Spillman and her husband on their land. Courtesy of Protect Grove City Crucially, these movements don’t break along party lines: Republicans, Democrats and Independents across the country are mad — and they’re working together to block development. This bipartisan push is particularly notable at a time of intense polarization. There’s not much that people from different political parties can agree on, but according to a recent poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, very few people want an A.I. data center in their community. That’s certainly true in Grove City, a Republican-leaning suburb of Columbus, where people of all parties opposed the Headwaters development. The nature of this coalition isn’t totally unprecedented, says Megan Mullin, a professor of public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles. “In so many ways, data center battles look like land use battles that have come before,” she says. “Battles over housing developments, wind farms or gas pipelines — we consistently see people come together across party lines to try to keep their community looking the way it’s always looked, and to fight back against what they perceive as harmful draws on community resources.” Mullin says a big difference now is that all of these hyper-local fights are happening at once. While one or two bipartisan coalitions on a land use debate wouldn’t rise to the level of national news, hundreds of them happening simultaneously around the country does. “That allows these local disputes to be connected to something national, and it also allows concrete movement building.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] In Ohio, residents of Grove City and the surrounding townships quickly mobilized once they realized that Headwaters wanted to site a data center in their community. “We got organized,” says Jen Belt, one of the four people behind Protect Grove City , which actively opposed the development. “Most people weren’t even aware that this was a thing. We taped flyers to every home within a three-mile radius of the developer’s site. We encouraged people to come to all of the council meetings.” They also worked on gathering signatures to encourage the Grove City city council to pass a moratorium. (Pleasant Township and Jackson Township had already passed moratoriums in the first half of 2026.) Ultimately, Belt says, they gathered more than 4,000 signatures for the online petition. Their efforts worked. In June, the city council passed a one-year moratorium on data center development. But Belt and her neighbors know it is temporary, and developers will come back once the year is up. So they have put a Community Consent Amendment (CCA) on the upcoming November ballot. If passed, it will require residents’ approval before any large-scale development can break ground. (While it’s geared toward data centers, it’s written to apply to all heavy industry.) Belt, like Spillman, lives in Pleasant Township, which she calls “suburban rural.” But she scoffs at the idea that the issue doesn’t impact her just because she’s not within city limits. “This is property that will be annexed from my town into Grove City,” says Belt, a registered Democrat. “It’s literally in my backyard. So it does affect us.” Spillman, a lifelong Republican, agrees: “This is our community. This is our neighborhood, and none of us can vote on any of this, because we don’t live in Grove City proper, but we still consider Grove City our home.” Data centers have been going up in earnest for the last decade, built to support the rapid growth of the cloud. Opposition has existed nearly as long . But as A.I. usage has exploded in the last several years, the demand for data centers has rapidly accelerated as well. The post Finally, Something Americans Agree On! appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: The cool, quiet hour after dawn feels like the best time to step outside in October, yet AIIMS says pollution stays highest in the early morning until about 8:30 or 9 am. Delhi's air shows how quickly things can turn. At 4 pm on Tuesday, 20 October, the Central Pollution Control Board put the Air Quality Index (AQI) at 179, which counts as moderate. By 7 am the next day, the Air Quality Early Warning System showed 219, which counts as poor, and it forecast 342 for 22 October. The invisible lid above the city The explanation lies in physics. Normally, temperature falls with height, so air near the ground mixes and carries pollutants upwards. University of Reading researchers Ankit Bhandekar and Laura Wilcox explain that a temperature inversion reverses this, placing warmer air above colder air like a lid on a pot. Pollutants stay near the ground, and the mixing height, the level up to which they can disperse, shrinks from about one kilometre in summer to a few hundred metres in winter. The lid sits lowest after dark. Sarath Guttikunda, founder of UrbanEmissions.Info, told Frontline that in November and December the inversion height can fall below 50 metres at night and hover around 200 to 500 metres by day. As the sun climbs, the layer lifts and the smog thins, which is why the early hours feel the worst. A bowl that holds on to smoke Delhi's geography makes this even worse. The city sits in the Indo-Gangetic plains, with the Himalayas to the north and the smaller Aravalli range to the south, which help create a natural bowl. Delhi's location between the Himalayas and the Aravallis, coupled with slow winds and little rain, allows pollution to linger. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) The Himalayas block air from flowing northward, so pollution must travel across northern India before it finds an exit over the Bay of Bengal. The monsoon rains that cleanse the air from July to September have gone by October, and winds slow down. Small shifts in weather can therefore tip the balance fast. Bhandekar and Wilcox note that on 5 January, 2025, favourable winds allowed authorities to lift some restrictions, yet by 15 January calmer winds and falling temperatures forced the city's strictest curbs. Delhi had not gained more cars, factories or construction sites from one week to the next. The Centre for Science and Environment also found something similar in winter 2023, when slow winds appeared to drive the most smog episodes in six years even though stubble fires in Punjab and Haryana nearly matched 2022. Solutions that follow the weather If weather decides when pollution turns, the Reading researchers argue, policy should follow the forecast rather than chase the smog. They suggest tightening construction restrictions when inversions are predicted, even on seemingly clear days, and designing measures for the whole Indo-Gangetic plains, since many of India's most polluted cities share the same conditions. Calm winds and falling temperatures can intensify smog even without an increase in vehicles, factories or construction. Photograph: ( The Print ) Delhi's Graded Response Action Plan already lets authorities act in advance on forecasts, with curbs ranging from dust control to limits on construction and vehicle movement. The other lever sits upwind, because smoke from stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana , where farmers clear fields quickly for wheat sowing, adds to the load each October and November. Some farmers avoid it by sowing wheat directly with a Happy Seeder , spraying a waste decomposer solution on straw , or selling paddy straw for conversion into fuel pellets . What you can do this season First, treat the cool early hours as the risky ones, since AIIMS advises staying indoors at peak hours and choosing indoor exercise over outdoor runs or cycling. Second, check the AQI daily on the SAMEER app, which AIIMS recommends, and wear an N95 mask if you step out. Third, take extra care of children, older people and anyone with heart or lung conditions, whom the AIIMS advisory flags as most at risk. Fourth, skip driving once a week to trim local emissions, as AIIMS suggests. The advice does not reach everyone equally. Business Standard reports that an air purifier costing ₹12,000 to ₹15,000 is out of reach for many informal workers, and that indoor air can still hold up to 70% of outdoor PM2.5 without sealed windows and purifiers. That is why forecast-led curbs and cleaner fields matter as much as personal habits. Delhi cannot change the bowl it sits in or the chill that settles each night, but it can change what it puts into the air beneath the lid. With poor air forecast for 21 to 23 October, the next crisp, quiet dawn is better read as a warning than a relief. Sources: 1. ' Delhi's air quality slips to poor category, forecast to worsen further ': by Akshita Singh for Business Standard, Published on 21 October, 2026 2. ' How weather patterns and faraway mountains make Delhi the world's most polluted megacity ': by Ankit Bhandekar and Laura Wilcox for The Conversation (republished by Newslaundry), Published on 3 March, 2025 3. ' Delhi's Air Pollution Explained! ': by R. Ramachandran for Frontline, Published on 9 December, 2016 4. ' Delhi's annual battle with air pollution: Aiims issues health advisory ': by Barkha Mathur for Business Standard, Published on 6 November, 2025 5. Η Εθνική Βιβλιοθήκη του Κοσόβου, γνωστή ως Εθνική και Πανεπιστημιακή Βιβλιοθήκη «Pjetër Bogdani», αποτελεί ένα από τα πιο χαρακτηριστικά δείγματα σύγχρονης αρχιτεκτονικής στα Βαλκάνια, προκαλώντας μέχρι σήμερα διαφορετικές αντιδράσεις για τον σχεδιασμό της. Ένα αρχιτεκτονικό έργο που διχάζει Το κτίριο σχεδιάστηκε από τον Κροάτη αρχιτέκτονα Andrija Mutnjaković και εγκαινιάστηκε στις 25 Νοεμβρίου 1982. Η κατασκευή του βασίστηκε σε έναν ασυνήθιστο συνδυασμό γεωμετρικών όγκων, με κυβικά τμήματα να ενώνονται κάτω από δεκάδες θόλους και ένα μεταλλικό δικτυωτό περίβλημα να καλύπτει την εξωτερική επιφάνεια. Η αρχιτεκτονική του συνδυάζει στοιχεία από τη βυζαντινή και την οθωμανική παράδοση της περιοχής με τις αρχές του μοντερνισμού. Οι θόλοι επιτρέπουν στο φυσικό φως να εισέρχεται στους εσωτερικούς χώρους, ενώ το μεταλλικό πλέγμα λειτουργεί ως σκίαστρο, περιορίζοντας την άμεση ηλιακή ακτινοβολία. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study Reading Time: 3 minutes A major five-year study finds that urban woodlands and mental health are closely connected, with well-kept city woods linked to fewer antidepressant prescriptions in Scotland’s poorest neighborhoods. Urban woodlands and mental health appear to move together, according to new research from the Universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow. Scientists tracked more than 129,000 people across Scotland over five years. They found that people living close to improved woodlands used less medication for depression and anxiety. The study , published in The Lancet Planetary Health, used National Health Service prescription records alongside census data. Researchers compared people living within a 10-minute walk of an upgraded woodland to those living farther away. The gap in medication use was substantial. People near a well-maintained, welcoming woodland were 10% less likely to be prescribed antidepressants. They were also 6% less likely to need anti-anxiety medication. That pattern held even after researchers accounted for income, demographics, and other factors known to affect mental health. This is one of the largest studies of its kind linking urban woodlands and mental health outcomes. The woodland upgrades came through Scottish Forestry’s Woods In and Around Towns program (WIAT). Funding paid for new footpaths, better signage, and community events in areas that needed it most. The program specifically targeted socially and financially disadvantaged communities. These are often the places with the least access to quality parks and green space to begin with. By focusing improvements there, researchers could measure whether fixing a woodland actually changed people’s health, not just their surroundings. What makes this research especially convincing is how it tracked people over time. When someone moved closer to an improved woodland, their need for medication tended to drop. When they moved farther away, that protective effect faded. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health was strengthened with a telling finding: when people moved closer to improved woodlands, their need for antidepressants fell, and when they moved away, the protective effect faded with them. Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Pexels. That detail matters. Earlier studies often compared different people living in different neighborhoods at a single moment. This approach made it hard to know whether nature improved mental health, or whether healthier people simply chose to live near woodlands already. By following the same individuals as their circumstances changed, researchers could rule out that explanation. Professor Catharine Ward Thompson, who led the study at the University of Edinburgh’s OPENspace Research Centre, said the findings offer stronger evidence on the link between urban woodlands and mental health than earlier research managed to provide. She added that the benefits may help reduce mental health inequalities across the population. Dr. Scott Ogletree, who carried out the analysis, said the project marks the first time mental health service data has been linked to a long-term national urban forestry program. He noted that relatively modest investments in local green space can meaningfully improve people’s wellbeing. Nature-based programs like WIAT, he said, can support broader efforts to improve mental health. The scale of the problem makes this evidence timely. Around one in eight people worldwide live with a mental health condition, and people in poorer communities are often hit hardest. These same communities often have the least access to high-quality woodlands and parks. Scotland’s government has pointed to this research as support for its wider environmental goals. Officials cited a target of creating 18,000 hectares of new woodland every year by 2029 to 2030. That commitment extends to urban tree planting aimed at improving air quality and quality of life. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health also fits into a broader pattern seen elsewhere, where community-driven tree planting has helped cool neighborhoods and improve public health by giving residents a direct role in restoring local green space. Programs like these suggest the benefits of investing in trees extend well beyond any single country. The research team behind the Scottish study has spent more than 20 years gathering evidence on the social value of local woodlands, working alongside Scottish Forestry and Forest Research. Their latest findings add a rigorous, long-term dataset to a growing conversation about nature-based public health policy. Funding came from the Economic and Social Research Council and the GroundsWell Consortium, a UK research partnership focused on how green and blue spaces reduce health inequalities. None of this suggests woodlands replace clinical care for depression or anxiety. What it does suggest is that a safe, welcoming patch of trees within walking distance can meaningfully shift the odds. As more cities weigh where to spend limited public money, the growing evidence on urban woodlands and mental health makes a strong case for choosing the trail over the parking lot. The post How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: What happens when two generations open their doors to one another? In West Philadelphia, a small but growing program called Second Story Collective is bringing college students and older residents together through shared housing, creating unexpected friendships along the way. For Ms. Julia, a retired nursing assistant who has lived in her neighborhood for more than 50 years, welcoming 22-year-old Drexel University student Jackson Tignor into her home has brought new companionship and laughter. In return, Jackson has found more than an affordable place to live -- he's discovered a sense of belonging and a deeper connection to the community around him. Through everyday moments of shared meals, conversations, and helping hands, the program is quietly challenging loneliness, housing insecurity, and the divisions that too often separate generations. Sometimes, building a stronger community begins with something as simple as opening a door.

items.descriptionOriginal: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

items.descriptionOriginal: At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, lunch was over and everyone was waiting for dessert. The thalis had been cleared, conversations had moved on, and there was only one thing left to do: bring out the kheer. Except this time, there was something unusual in the cutlery. Niki Rai, who had organised the gathering, asked her guests to hold on to their spoons instead of throwing them away. A few eyebrows went up. She had already told everyone that these were edible, but people were still understandably unsure. Then came dessert. "Now this is your biscuit," Rai told the children, handing them their dessert with the spoon. The reaction was almost immediate. The children started biting into the spoons, treating them less like cutlery and more like a crunchy snack. The adults were more hesitant, watching first to see if it really worked. Soon, however, others wanted a taste too. "It was quite a spectacle, but it was worth it," Rai recalls. The spoons had been made by Mumbai-based startup Edybites, which is trying to tackle a very ordinary problem: what happens to a disposable spoon after the few minutes it spends helping us finish a meal? Its answer is simple enough to eat. Founded by Rupesh K Sanghvi in 2022, Edybites makes edible spoons using a millet and flour-based formulation. The idea is that the spoon can become part of the meal rather than another piece of waste to be thrown away. If it is not eaten, the product is designed to naturally decompose. After 88 failed attempts, Sanghvi refined the spoon's shape, texture and sturdiness to make it practical for everyday use. But turning that simple idea into a spoon that could hold its own through a meal was another story. It had to be sturdy enough to carry food, pleasant enough to eat and practical enough to make at a price people would accept. The idea began with a spoon and a piece of khakra For Sanghvi, the thought first came during the COVID-19 lockdown. With fewer services and errands available, everyday household work suddenly meant doing much more oneself. One day, after preparing a meal and looking at a sink full of utensils, he found himself eating with his fingers because there was no clean spoon left. That brought back a familiar Gujarati food memory: khakra. "If we can finish our last meal of dal khichdi with a combination of khakra," he thought, could something similar be made in the form of a spoon? The thought stayed with him. It also connected with something Sanghvi had observed during his more than 17 years in the aviation and travel industry. Having worked in sales and business development with airlines including Malaysia Airlines, Flydubai, Malindo Air and Kuwait Airways, he had seen how much disposable material moved through a flight. Once a flight landed, used food packaging and cutlery had to be discarded. Some meal components could not be reused because of safety and airline policies, even when they had not been consumed. The edible spoons are designed to hold food during a meal and can be eaten afterwards, reducing the need for disposable plastic cutlery. For Sanghvi, that raised a broader question : could at least one small part of the meal be made differently? He initially imagined the spoon being used with yoghurt, pastries, desserts or dishes such as dal khichdi and sambar rice on flights. Aviation remains one of the sectors he is interested in, alongside hospitals, institutional catering and events. The larger idea, however, is not simply to tell people to use less plastic. It is to make the alternative convenient enough that people actually use it. Making a spoon that does not fall apart That turned out to be the difficult part. Sanghvi says he failed 88 times while developing the spoon. Each version had to be tested for its shape, size, weight, and sturdiness. It needed to be strong enough to hold food, but not so hard that eating it became uncomfortable. The formulation uses a combination of sorghum, corn flour, and wheat flour, along with other ingredients. Sanghvi says the precise recipe is proprietary, but the millet and flour-based formulation is central to giving the spoon its structure. Too much flour, and the spoon could become soggy quickly. Too much firmness, and it could become difficult to bite. The team also experimented with flavours. Chocolate emerged as one of the main variants, particularly because it pairs naturally with vanilla ice cream. Edybites offers different flavours, including chocolate, which pairs well with desserts such as vanilla ice cream. That makes dessert one of the easiest places to introduce the concept. A person may be more willing to eat a spoon after finishing a bowl of ice cream than rethink every piece of cutlery used during an entire meal. There is also a practical reason Edybites has focused on spoons rather than trying to replace every disposable food item at once. Sanghvi says other edible products, such as cups, can face challenges when they are expected to hold liquids for longer periods. With tea or coffee, for instance, the material can soften or affect the eating experience. The spoon offers a smaller, more manageable starting point. The product has a shelf life of about three months without refrigeration, with the team working towards extending it further. It is made under a contractual manufacturing arrangement, with attention to hygiene and the heating process required to form the spoon. The finished spoons are individually covered and packed in boxes designed to minimise breakage during transportation. The product also requires the relevant food safety certification, including an FSSAI licence. When the spoon reached a real dining table For Niki Rai, the real test came not in a product demonstration but at a family gathering. Rai, a learning and development professional and executive coach, had first heard about the product through a friend. She was curious but wanted to try it herself before recommending it to others. When she eventually used Edybites spoons at a Ganpati gathering, she served them alongside a regular thali and asked guests to try them with the sabzi. Later, she brought them out again with kheer. The children needed little convincing. "For kids, it was like a biscuit," she says. For adults, the experience was more about getting used to the idea. Rai says the spoon felt similar to a regular spoon and was comfortable to use, although its smaller size meant it could not hold a large quantity of food. She found it particularly suited to desserts, while children could use it for foods such as porridge too. At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, Niki Rai introduced Edybites spoons to guests, with children happily biting into them like biscuits after dessert. What stood out most to her was not just that the spoon was edible, but that it did not feel like a compromise. For Rai, taste was important. She also liked that the ingredients included grains such as jowar and wheat, along with fenugreek, rather than making the spoon feel like an entirely separate object that happened to be sustainable. Once the children started eating theirs, curiosity took over. The parents who had initially been apprehensive began joining in. Soon, Rai says, people were asking for extra spoons. Since then, she has continued recommending the product at events and gatherings, including while travelling. Making the sustainable choice practical There is, however, a catch. An Edybites spoon currently costs around Rs 7-8, according to Sanghvi. That is considerably more than a conventional disposable spoon, making price one of the biggest hurdles to getting people to make the switch. After all, when a plastic spoon costs a fraction of that, convincing someone to pay more for something they will eat or discard after one meal is not easy. Sanghvi has seen this play out in the conversations around the product. "However rich you are, at one point you would think, just to have a spoon, why should I pay seven rupees?" he says. That is why Edybites has not tried to rush into the mass market. Since November last year, when the startup began seeing stronger market traction, it has sold or distributed more than 5,100 spoons. For now, Sanghvi is taking a gradual route, exploring events, institutional catering, hospitals and airlines, along with markets where customers may be more willing to pay for sustainable alternatives. Edybites spoons blend sorghum, corn and wheat flour to create a sturdy yet easy-to-bite alternative to plastic cutlery. There is another irony to solve, too. The spoon is edible, but it still needs to reach the customer intact. That means packaging it carefully against moisture and breakage. Sanghvi says the team is experimenting with paper-based packaging and ways to reduce plastic without compromising the product. For a startup trying to eliminate one disposable item, using plastic to protect that alternative is hardly an ideal solution. It is a problem the team is still working through. What happens when a spoon becomes part of the meal? Perhaps the most interesting thing about Edybites is that its sustainability pitch does not end with the word "biodegradable". It asks people to rethink what they consider waste in the first place. A conventional spoon has a very short life. It may spend a few minutes carrying a bite of food before being separated from the meal and sent to a bin. Edybites is trying to stretch that experience a little further: what if the spoon itself became the final bite? At scale, that could add up. Based on an estimated 2.5-3 grams of plastic in a conventional disposable spoon, Edybites estimates that every one lakh edible spoons could potentially displace around 250-300 kg of single-use plastic. At 10 lakh spoons, that works out to roughly 2.5-3 tonnes of potential plastic displacement. These are estimates of what could be displaced if the edible spoons replace plastic ones at that scale, rather than plastic waste already avoided by the startup. For Sanghvi, however, the number is only one part of the larger picture. He is particularly interested in what happens when children encounter such alternatives early. His hope is that edible or biodegradable options could eventually find their way into school canteens, hospitals, senior-care facilities and other places where disposable cutlery is used every day. And perhaps that is where Rai's Ganpati gathering offers a glimpse of what adoption can look like. Edybites has sold or distributed over 5,100 spoons and estimates that replacing one lakh plastic spoons could potentially prevent 250–300 kg of single-use plastic waste. The children simply needed to know they could eat the spoon. Once they did, the idea stopped being a sustainability lesson and became something much more familiar: a biscuit-like treat at the end of a meal. Rai has continued recommending the spoons at gatherings since that first experience, and her reason is simple. "We've got to be a flag bearer in our own way, no matter how small that change is," she says. For now, Edybites is still figuring out how to make that small change cheaper, easier to package, and practical at a much larger scale. But somewhere between a Mumbai kitchen, 88 failed attempts and a group of children happily chomping through their spoons after dessert, the idea has found its most convincing test yet. The spoon did not end up in the bin, it ended up being dessert. All images courtesy of Edybites team

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most people moving through a train station aren’t really paying attention. They’re somewhere between where they left and where they’re going, phone out, eyes on the platform. Putting art there is an interesting bet; you’re trying to get someone to stop and look at something that might surprise and delight them, and that they had no intention of seeking out. NJ Transit has been doing this since 2019, when it launched the TRANSITional Art Project as a pilot at Newark Penn Station. Working with the New Jersey State Council on the Arts , it has since installed temporary exhibitions of murals and photography by New Jersey artists at seven more stations. The latest is now at Morris Plains Rail Station: a show called “ Tracks Through Time: Movement, History and Human Connection .” A show about the tracks themselves The subject matter has good timing. The exhibition looks at 250 years of American history through the lens of railroads , in the very stations where people still depend on those rails to get to work. It includes photography by Beyti Barbaros, murals by Jonathan Yumi, and a three-panel mural installation by Catherine Thurston. “Railroads helped to build this nation,” said NJ Transit President and CEO Kris Kolluri, “and as we mark 250 years of our shared history, there’s no better place to tell that story than in the very stations where the past and daily life intersect.” Art you don’t have to go looking for Nobody goes to a train station specifically to see art, but that might be at the heart of the reasoning for this whole project. Most people at a gallery already decided they wanted to be there. The commuter who glances up at a mural while waiting for the 8:14 didn’t, and that’s a different kind of encounter. Danielle Bursk, the New Jersey State Arts Council Director of Community Partnerships & Artist Services, put it this way: “Public art has the power to transform the places we move through every day into places where we can pause, connect , and see our communities in new ways.” The program also pays the artists. Some participants receive stipends toward the cost of developing a project in a transit space, which matters given how rarely public art comes with any budget at all. The program has now reached eight stations: Newark, Camden, Atlantic City, Trenton, New Brunswick, Summit, Rahway, and Morris Plains. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Columbia University Medical Center wanted to answer a specific question: what is the least amount of movement needed to offset the effects of prolonged sitting ? In 2023, they tested a range of options and found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy. Not a longer walk once an hour. Not standing more. The answer was as short and sweet as five minutes, every half hour. When NPR’s Body Electric ran that same challenge with more than 20,000 listeners, participants reported higher productivity and lower fatigue. Those results have real implications: adults in the United States average 9.5 hours of sitting per day, and the research linking prolonged sitting to fatigue, weight gain, back pain , and chronic disease is extensive. The five-minute walk is the most surprising and accessible finding, but there are four other adjustments, drawn from physical therapists, a biomechanist, and a professional ergonomist, that address what walking breaks alone can’t fix. For back pain: a three-dimensional spine rotation Slouching at a desk doesn’t just feel uncomfortable; it puts sustained stress on the middle section of the spine. Vinh Pham , a physical therapist, recommends a move he calls the 3D T-spine rotation. Stand and drop your right foot behind your left, about a foot apart. Hold your right arm straight up and your left arm behind you, as if shaking the hand of someone behind you. Then simultaneously drop both arms and twist toward your right foot, keeping them straight throughout. Return to the starting position, hold for two seconds, and repeat ten times before switching sides. The goal isn’t stretching in the conventional sense. It’s to get the spine comfortable with its full range of motion — side bending, backward bending, rotating — so those movements don’t cause pain when they come up in ordinary life. For eye strain: look somewhere else Digital eye strain happens when the eyes spend hours focused at close range. They turn inward to track a nearby screen, adjust their focus for short vision, and hold that position. Eye doctors say the result is often fatigue, headaches, or blurred vision. The simplest intervention is the one most people already know and skip: look away from the screen and focus on something distant. A full eye-muscle stretch goes further. That means moving your gaze deliberately through different positions to work muscles that stay locked during screen time . For restlessness: stop trying to find the right posture Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position , is direct on the idea that fidgeting is a signal, not a bad habit. It means your body needs to stop holding a static position, regardless of how ergonomically correct that position might be. Bowman and physical therapist Leada Malek , author of Science of Stretch , share a phrase common in their field: “Your best posture is your next posture.” Any position, held long enough, creates strain. The goal isn’t to find the correct one and maintain it; it’s to keep moving between positions. Sitting, standing, reclining, shifting. “Adaptive and dynamic,” as Malek describes it, and easy to move in and out of. For shoulder and neck aches: fix the monitor height first Professional ergonomist Meg Honan identifies one setup problem that causes more widespread discomfort than almost anything else: the “head down, arms up” configuration, where the screen is too low and the keyboard is too high. Bring your screen to eye level using books, a stand, or whatever is available. Lower your keyboard and mouse so you’re not shrugging to type. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, an external keyboard lets you lower your arms without losing screen height. Honan describes the head-down, arms-up position as a reliable setup for feeling “achy, sore and tired.” Getting the monitor to eye level is the single adjustment with the most downstream effect. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 5 research-backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Reading Time: 2 minutes 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Making your home more sustainable doesn’t require expensive renovations or a complete lifestyle overhaul. In fact, some of the most effective changes are surprisingly simple, and you can start making them today. From the products you use to clean your kitchen to the materials you sleep under, everyday household choices can affect the environment. If you want to reduce waste, embrace more natural materials, and make your home a little greener, here are five sustainable swaps to consider. 1. Swap Disposable Cleaning Products for Reusable Alternatives Consider how many paper towels, disposable wipes, and plastic cleaning bottles you use in a typical month. These everyday essentials can create surprising waste, especially when you replace them constantly. Instead, consider switching to washable microfiber cloths, reusable cleaning pads, and refillable spray bottles . You can also explore concentrated cleaning solutions that require less packaging and are designed to be diluted at home. These small changes can reduce household waste while helping you save money over time. 2. Choose Natural Bedding Over Synthetic Materials Your bedroom is another great place to introduce more sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Many conventional comforters contain synthetic polyester fillings derived from petroleum-based materials, which can contribute to plastic pollution. Replacing them with natural alternatives is a more environmentally conscious choice. An organic wool comforter offers a natural filling that provides warmth while allowing air to circulate and helping regulate temperature throughout the night. Wool is also renewable and biodegradable when untreated, making it an appealing option for anyone looking to reduce reliance on synthetic textiles. Your bedroom is a great place to introduce sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Image: Home of Wool 3. Replace Single-Use Kitchen Products The kitchen is often one of the biggest sources of household waste, but it’s also one of the easiest places to make sustainable improvements. Instead of relying on plastic wrap, disposable sandwich bags, and single-use food containers, invest in reusable alternatives. Glass storage containers, washable silicone bags, and beeswax food wraps can help you cut down on unnecessary packaging. You could also swap disposable coffee pods for a reusable coffee filter or French press. Over time, these changes can noticeably reduce how much waste leaves your kitchen. 4. Switch to Energy-Efficient Lighting If you’re still using traditional incandescent light bulbs, switching to LED alternatives is a straightforward way to reduce household energy consumption. LED bulbs use significantly less electricity and generally last much longer than incandescent bulbs, so you need to replace them less often. This can help lower both your electricity bills and your home’s environmental footprint. You can also make better use of natural daylight by keeping windows unobstructed and arranging furniture to maximize available sunlight. 5. Choose Refillable Bathroom Essentials Bathrooms can quickly accumulate plastic packaging, particularly from shampoo, conditioner, hand soap, and body wash bottles. Switch to refillable products or solid alternatives, such as shampoo bars and bar soaps. Many brands now offer concentrated refills, so you can reuse existing containers instead of buying new plastic bottles every time. You might also replace disposable cotton rounds with washable alternatives and choose toothbrushes with replaceable heads to cut unnecessary waste. Start with one or two manageable swaps, build on them gradually, and you’ll soon discover that sustainable living can be both practical and rewarding. The post 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have developed a new way to quickly recycle electronic waste. Many electronic devices use flame-retardant plastic as casing in order to reduce the risk of electrical fires. This plastic is formulated using a metal called antimony along with organic bromide compounds. In fact, 39% of the world’s antimony is used to create flame-retardant plastics, most of which will eventually end up as part of the tens of millions of tons of electronic waste generated each year. Rice University’s James Tour recently published a study in Nature Chemical Engineering detailing an improved method to recover antimony from this electronic waste stream. “Antimony is a critical metal with a constrained supply,” says Tour, a professor of chemistry and corresponding author on the study. “My research team has adapted our flash Joule heating technique to quickly and effectively recover antimony from this plastic waste stream.” To recapture antimony from the plastic, it first has to be released from the plastic. This is, chemically, a challenging step. As the antimony is released, other toxic compounds, organic bromides, can form that are difficult to capture. “Conventionally heating the plastic releases the antimony in a volatile and difficult to collect form as well as creating and releasing hazardous organic bromide compounds,” says Leo Haoxin Ye, the first author of this paper and a graduate student at Rice. “Other options are risky or more impractical, such as using strong acids, organic solvents, or multistep treatment options.” The issue, the team thought, could be with the slowness of conventional heating, which allowed the elements to change forms or create new compounds. If they could adapt Tour’s flash Joule heating, which heats materials up to hundreds of degrees Celsius in a manner of milliseconds, they might be able to avoid some of the pitfalls of conventional heating while still releasing the antimony from the plastic. “We found flame-retardant plastic waste generated by our own laboratory, ground it up, and then placed it between two sheets of electrically heated carbon paper. We used ultrafast heating to pulse-heat it several times,” Ye says. “Then we held the plastic briefly at a high temperature, which allowed the antimony to evaporate and condense in a collection area.” The method, called isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating, was tested on three different types of flame-retardant plastic: a power-supply housing, a printed circuit board, and an electrical connector. From these, the team was able to recover approximately 90% of the antimony, while converting 83% of the bromide into hydrogen bromide, an inorganic compound that, while hazardous, is a valuable industrial chemical that can be captured with sodium hydroxide to form a stable salt. And the number of organic bromide compounds produced dramatically reduced, a result of the flash Joule heating’s speed. The plastic spent only 9.4 milliseconds in between 200-500 degrees Celsius, the temperature range in which organic bromide compounds form. “Isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating could improve the speed, safety, and practicality of antimony recovery from discarded flame-retardant plastics,” Tour says. “Given that the world is on track to produce 82 million metric tons of flame-retardant plastic waste by 2030, this represents an important step forward to conserving and reusing our critical antimony supply while also regenerating bromide salts for reuse.” This research was funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the US Army Corps of Engineers, ERDC. Source: Rice University The post New method can quickly recycle electronic waste appeared first on Futurity .

items.title: Τα ανθρώπινα νευρικά βλαστοκύτταρα είναι ευαίσθητα στις παραλλαγές του ιού COVID

items.description: Τα ανθρώπινα νευρικά βλαστοκύτταρα που βοηθούν στο σχηματισμό του εγκεφάλου και του νωτιαίου μυελού είναι πολύ ευαίσθητα στον SARS-CoV-2, συμπεριλαμβανομένων των παραλλαγών BA.1 και BA.2 του Omicron, σύμφωνα με νέα έρευνα. Τα ευρήματα εγείρουν ανησυχίες σχετικά με τις πιθανές επιπτώσεις της μητρικής λοίμωξης COVID-19 στην πρώιμη ανάπτυξη του νευρικού συστήματος και υπογραμμίζουν τη σημασία της παρακολούθησης των παιδιών πρώην…
items.descriptionOriginal: Human neural stem cells that help form the brain and spinal cord are highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2, including Omicron variants BA.1 and BA.2, according to new research. The findings raise concerns about the potential effects of maternal COVID-19 infection on early nervous system development and underscore the importance of monitoring children exposed to the virus before birth. The researchers, led by Prue Talbot, a professor of the graduate division in the Department of Molecular, Cell and Systems Biology, found that human neural stem cells were significantly more susceptible to infection by SARS-CoV-2 spike pseudoparticles—modified, non-replicating virus particles used to safely study infection—than undifferentiated human embryonic stem cells. The susceptibility was observed with the original viral spike as well as the two Omicron variants. “Our data clearly show that human neural stem cells are readily infected by SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus, including the currently prevalent Omicron variants,” Talbot says. Neural stem cells emerge from the ectoderm, an early embryonic tissue that gives rise to the central nervous system. Because these cells help establish the foundation for the brain and spinal cord, infection during early development could have consequences ranging from pregnancy loss and severe developmental abnormalities to more subtle changes that may not be apparent at birth. “Such subtle damage might only appear years later as learning, behavioral, or cognitive difficulties,” says Ann Song, a postdoctoral researcher in Talbot’s lab and the first author of the study in PLOS One . The transmission of SARS-CoV-2 from mother to fetus has been documented, including during the first trimester. Children exposed to the virus in utero are now reaching ages at which potential neurodevelopmental differences can be assessed. The researchers also noted that their findings are consistent with a large health-record study linking maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection to an increased risk of a neurodevelopmental diagnosis in children by age 3. To investigate how the virus might enter developing neural cells, the team differentiated human embryonic stem cells into neural stem cells and exposed them to the pseudoparticles. The experiments showed that Omicron pseudoparticles entered neural stem cells primarily through endocytosis, a process in which cells engulf external material. The researchers found that blocking this pathway with the compound filipin reduced viral entry by approximately 75% to 85%. The team also found that neural stem cells have a relatively sparse layer of sugar molecules on their surfaces. Removing these sugar groups increased pseudoparticle entry twofold to fourfold, suggesting that the cell-surface sugar layer may help limit viral access. The research addresses a question that cannot readily be investigated through experiments in pregnant women: whether early precursors of the nervous system are vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2. Although fetal transmission has been documented, the susceptibility of these early developmental cells has been less clear. “Our data emphasize the need for monitoring children exposed in utero to SARS-CoV-2 for evidence of deficiencies in the central nervous system,” Song says. Talbot says the findings do not establish that infection of neural stem cells by the pseudovirus causes neurological harm in human pregnancies. “Further research will be needed to determine whether and how infection at these early stages affects brain development,” she says. The study was funded by a UCR Academic Senate Committee on Research grant, an Academic Merit Fellowship, a Yvonne Danielson Endowed Graduate Award, a UCR Graduate Division Dissertation Completion Fellowship Award, and the Tobacco-Related Disease Research Program. Source: UC Riverside The post Human neural stem cells are susceptible to COVID virus variants appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: He’s the first Indian to win the Oskar Klein Medal, yet he still cycles to work. His story is as much about simplicity as it is about extraordinary scientific achievement. Meet Kolkata-born theoretical physicist Ashoke Sen, whose pioneering research in string theory and black hole physics has helped shape our understanding of the universe. After studying at Presidency College and IIT Kanpur and pursuing doctoral research in the United States, he returned to India to continue his scientific journey. In 2012, Sen received the $3 million Fundamental Physics Prize for his contributions to string theory. In 2026, he made history by becoming the first Indian physicist to receive the Oskar Klein Medal, recognising his influential work in theoretical physics. Despite global recognition and some of the field’s highest honours, Sen’s story reminds us that scientific greatness is measured by curiosity, dedication and the ideas we contribute, not by outward displays of success. His journey continues to inspire young Indians to pursue knowledge and push the boundaries of human understanding. Know a student who’s drawn to physics? items.titleOriginal: 'I Spent 4 Years Farming on Weekends. Here Are 7 Things to Know Before Starting Your Own Organic Farm'
items.description: Για χρόνια, ο Deepak Sabharwal γνώριζε το φαγητό σε μεγάλο βαθμό από την άλλη πλευρά του τραπεζιού. Είχε περάσει σχεδόν δύο δεκαετίες στον εταιρικό κόσμο, συνεργαζόμενος με εταιρείες όπως η General Electric (GE), η PepsiCo και η Tata. Οι μέρες του αφορούσαν συναντήσεις, αριθμούς και ανάπτυξη. Η γεωργία ήταν κάτι που περνούσε χρόνο κάνοντας τα Σαββατοκύριακα, στις φάρμες της οικογένειάς του στο Pushkar, R.…
items.descriptionOriginal: For years, Deepak Sabharwal knew food largely from the other side of the table. He had spent nearly two decades in the corporate world, working with companies such as General Electric (GE), PepsiCo, and Tata. His days were about meetings, numbers, and growth. Farming was something he spent time doing on weekends, at his family's farms in Pushkar, Rajasthan. Then one day, he noticed the pesticides being used on his own farm . Around the same time, his mother was diagnosed with cancer. The two things came together in his mind in a way he could not ignore. "I began wondering what we were really eating every day, and that was a simple but uncomfortable question to ask," he tells The Better India . That question eventually took him from boardrooms to fields. His hands-on farming journey began in 2012, while he was still working at GE, and he spent almost four years travelling to Pushkar on weekends to learn farming and experiment on his family's land. Today, he is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited . The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making produce grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers more accessible to urban families. Deepak wanted Earthy Tales to do more than sell vegetables. For the co-founder, it was about fixing a disconnect he had begun to see between the soil, the farmer, and the person eventually eating the food. Years of working closely with farmers taught him that organic farming involves much more than avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. Here are seven lessons he wishes anyone entering the space would understand. 1. Start with the soil It is tempting to begin a farming business by asking one question. What should I grow? Deepak believes there is another question that should come first. What is the condition of my soil? Today, Deepak is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land, and finding out which chemicals may have been used there. Because for him, organic farming does not begin with a label. It begins underground. "Organic farming begins with soil, not with certification or branding," he says. A healthy farm may require compost, organic matter, mulching, natural inputs, better water management and, where appropriate, livestock integration. The aim is to move away from synthetic pesticides and fertilisers while gradually rebuilding the health of the land. That is also why he advises beginners not to convert an entire farm at once. He suggests starting with a small patch, trying a crop and observing how it performs over one or two cycles before taking the bigger plunge. After all, the soil has its own pace. A business plan cannot always make it move faster. 2. Build the whole system One of his early assumptions was that organic farming was largely about avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. He soon realised how incomplete that understanding was. Seed selection, soil health, water, compost, livestock, pest management, crop planning, harvesting, grading, storage, and transport all become part of the equation. "Natural farming is not only about not using chemicals. It is a complete system," he says. And the work does not end when the crop leaves the field. It has to be sorted, packed, and transported. Some produce will be damaged. Some will not look perfect. Some may not sell in time. All of that has a cost. For someone starting, this is an important reality to understand. You are not simply starting a farm. You are building a system around that farm. 3. Earn farmer trust Getting a farmer to change the way they have farmed for years is not as easy as giving them a training session. Deepak learnt this by working closely with farmers. A farmer cannot treat a crop as an experiment. A crop failure can mean a family's income is affected. So when someone asks a farmer to reduce their reliance on synthetic pesticides or change farming practices, the farmer needs more than promises. "Farmers do not trust speeches. They trust consistency," he adds. The aim is not only to stop using chemicals, but to gradually rebuild the health of the land. That consistency can mean repeated visits to the farm, helping identify pests, discussing what to do when a crop begins to fail , providing training and, most importantly, helping create a market for what the farmer grows. At Earthy Tales, the approach has involved working closely with farmers and supporting them in moving towards natural farming methods that rely less on synthetic inputs. The lesson is particularly important for entrepreneurs who want to work with farmers. If you want farmers to take a risk with you, you have to be willing to share some of that risk. 4. Find buyers first This was another lesson that took the co-founder time to learn. In farming, it is easy to fall in love with the idea of growing something. But a good crop does not automatically become a good business. "Natural farming must be market-linked. Otherwise, the farmer carries all the risk," he says. So before sowing, an entrepreneur needs to think about the customer. What does the customer buy regularly? What can the region grow reliably? What price is realistic? How far does the produce need to travel? Who will buy it? At Earthy Tales, he noticed that many customers first came looking for fresh fruits and vegetables. Once they developed confidence in the source, they began buying everyday staples such as atta, pulses, oils, spices, and ghee. The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making chemical-free food more accessible to urban families. That taught him something important about building a food business. Trust usually comes before the larger basket. A farmer may produce something excellent. But if there is no reliable buyer at the other end, the farmer still carries the risk. The market, therefore, cannot be an afterthought. It has to be part of the crop plan from the beginning. 5. Plan for uncertainty This sounds obvious, but it is one of the hardest realities for a business-minded newcomer to accept. Nature does not work according to demand forecasts. A farmer can plan for a crop, only for rain, heat, pests, or disease to change the outcome. Even when the crop does well, demand may not arrive at the same pace. Deepak remembers believing in the early days that good produce would naturally find its way to customers. "I believed that if we had good produce, the rest would follow," he says. "But food does not work like that." A crop arrives when it is ready, not when the customer wants it. It also creates a risk of wastage. Produce can be rejected because it is bruised, oddly shaped, or simply because there is more of it than the market needs that week. For a new entrepreneur, planning for unpredictable harvests and demand is essential. Crop cycles, storage and transport need to be flexible enough to handle surplus produce or unexpected delays. The more fragile the system, the more one bad season can hurt. 6. Know your numbers There is a natural temptation to think that a business built around a good cause will eventually work itself out. The co-founder has learnt otherwise. Organic farming can involve higher planning requirements, uncertain yields, wastage, packaging costs, logistics and working capital. If these numbers are ignored, even a business with the right intentions can struggle. "You cannot build a farmer-first business if the business itself is not financially sustainable," he says. That does not mean reducing farming to profit margins. It means understanding that farmers cannot be supported by a business that keeps losing money. For him, the lesson is to calculate what each sale really costs, from sourcing and packaging to transport and wastage, before deciding whether the business can grow. The goal is to find a balance where the customer gets trustworthy food, the farmer gets a fairer return, and the business remains strong enough to keep going. 7. Give it time Perhaps the biggest investment an aspiring organic farmer needs is not money. It is patience. Soil may take time to recover . Farmers may take time to trust a new method. Customers may take time to change their buying habits. And a young business may take years before its systems begin to settle. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land. The co-founder knows this personally. His own journey began with weekend trips to Pushkar while he was still working full time. For almost four years, he travelled between his corporate job and the farm, slowly learning what it meant to grow food. A good farm needs more than good crops "Patience is not optional in this business. It is part of the model," he says. That patience is also needed when things go wrong. A farmer may have a poor harvest. A crop may not sell. A transition may take longer than expected. A customer may question the price. The temptation is to look for a shortcut. But Deepak's experience has taught him that there are very few shortcuts when you are trying to change something as fundamental as how food is grown. Deepak's journey from corporate offices to farming has given him a broader view of an organic farming business. Growing crops without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers is only part of the work. The rest is making sure farmers earn a fair return, produce reaches customers and the business can keep going. For him, Earthy Tales is an attempt to bring soil health, farmer livelihoods and consumer wellbeing together. And for anyone thinking of starting an organic farming business, the question goes beyond how much they can grow. It is whether they can build a system in which the soil, the farmer and the customer all have a reason to stay. All pictures courtesy Deepak Sabharwal.
